Milchamot ha-Shem 2:1–2:34. Select a Hebrew word for its morphology, lemma, root, senses and the comments anchored to it. A dotted underline marks a word a commentator quotes.

2:1

The Wars of the LORD

The-Wars-of the-LORD

Grammar
  • מלחמות is a construct plural, 'wars of'; the Name that follows is the Tetragrammaton, read 'the LORD'.
  • The title is taken from Num 21:14, 'the book of the Wars of the LORD', and is given in English as the decisions give it.

Title of the book (decisions: Names and titles).

Apparatus
  • Num 21:14: 'the book of the Wars of the LORD', the source of the title.
  • Base text: the Wikisource witness, not yet collated against the 1931 scan (open question 2); any Wikisource addition is translated as base text.
2:2

Question: one of the students asked, and these are his words: "Let our teacher inform us: the worship and the prayer that we pray, to whom it pertains. To the Cause of causes, blessed be He, or to the emanated being that was emanated from Him (Ze'ir Anpin), as explained to us in your hearing by our teacher Salem son of David, who travelled from here to the Holy Land, according to the true faith, as explained in the book Matzref ha-Emunah and in a book on the Torah, that whoever worships Ein Sof worships without a God of truth and without a God of judgment, so that we may know whom we shall worship. And your reply, speedily, my lord. Thus far."

asking asked one of the-students and-these-are-his-words let-inform-us our-teacher the-worship and-the-prayer that-we pray to-whom it-pertains to-the-Cause-of causes blessed-be-He or to-the-emanated-being that was-emanated from-Him Ze'ir-Anpin as explained to-us in-your-hearing our-teacher Salem son of-David who-travelled from-here to-the-land of-the-Holy according-to the-faith the-true as-explained in-the-book Matzref ha-Emunah and-in-a-book on-the-Torah that-whoever-worships to-Ein Sof worships without a-God-of truth and-without a-God-of judgment so-that we-may-know - whom we-shall-worship and-your-reply speedily my-lord thus-far

Grammar
  • שאול שאל is an infinitive absolute before a finite verb: 'asking, he asked'. The heading of the correspondence is 'Question' (decisions).
  • וז״ל introduces the quotation, which runs to ע״כ at the end; the question is one long quoted sentence-chain.
  • The question offers two objects of worship joined by או, 'or': the Cause of causes, or the emanated being. The או sets them as alternatives.
  • שהעובד לאין סוף עובד ללא אלהי אמת: the participle שהעובד is the subject, 'whoever worships Ein Sof', and the verb repeats as 'worships'.
  • כדי שנדע את מי נעבוד: את is the object marker before מי, 'whom'; the purpose clause closes the question.

The quotation runs from וז״ל to ע״כ. The parentheses around ז״א are the writer's and stay in parentheses inside the quotation.

Apparatus
  • 2 Chr 15:3: 'לְלֹא אֱלֹהֵי אֱמֶת', 'without the true God', is echoed in ללא אלהי אמת (2:2.49-51); the English keeps 'without a God of truth'.
  • Isa 30:18: 'כִּי אֱלֹהֵי מִשְׁפָּט ה׳', 'for the LORD is a God of judgment', is echoed in אלהי משפט (2:2.53-54).
  • עה״ת (2:2.44) is read as על התורה, 'on the Torah'. It occurs only here, and the work it names is not identified.
2:3

Reply. "Your reply is explained in the book Kisse Eliyahu, from folio 13 to folio 18: 'A wise man will hear and add to learning.' And what we have received is that worship is to God, one Lord, in order to draw the flow from Him to the ten sefirot, as Lechem Shlomo wrote. Thus far the words of the respondent."

Reply your-reply is-explained in-the-book Kisse Eliyahu from-folio 13 to folio 18 will-hear a-wise-man and-will-add to-learning and-what-is-received by-us that-worship to-God lord one in-order-to-draw the-flow from-Him to ten sefirot as wrote Lechem Shlomo thus-far the-respondent

Grammar
  • The reply is the respondent's letter, quoted in double marks from 'Your reply' to the closing 'Thus far'; the verse inside it is in single marks.
  • ישמע חכם ויוסף לקח is Prov 1:5, quoted without a formula. The yiqtol ישמע is read as the verse's future, 'will hear'.
  • והמקובל בידינו שהעבודה לאל אדון אחד: the participle phrase is the subject of 'is that worship is to one Lord'; the English puts it first.
  • להמשיך השפע ממנו אל עשר ספירות: the infinitive gives the purpose of the worship, to draw the flow from Him to the ten sefirot.
  • כמו שכתב לחם שלמה: 'as Lechem Shlomo wrote'; a book cited by its title, with no reference given.

The respondent's answer to the question in 2:2; its closing formula עכ״ל closes the quotation.

Other readings (1)
  • ישמע חכם ויוסף לקח: Let the wise man hear and add to learning jussive the yiqtol read as a wish, not as the future of the verse
Apparatus
  • Prov 1:5 (2:3.12–15): 'A wise man will hear and add to learning'.
2:4

The questioner replied again. Your reply, my friend, came closed and sealed, and in it there is nothing but an indication of a place: "to study in Kisse Eliyahu, from folio 13 to folio 18, 'A wise man will hear and add to learning,' and what we have received is that worship is to God, one Lord, etc." I did not understand your opinion and your intention in this, whether this, what you have received, is in accordance with the words of Kisse Eliyahu or the opposite of his words. For when I studied in Kisse Eliyahu the place you marked for me, I did not find what I sought; on the contrary, there, on folio 3, he compares the oneness of the Creator to the other kinds of oneness, where he wrote: "Just as this house as a whole is called by the name one house. And if you enter it, you will find many rooms, large and small, and many other places. And each and every one of them ascribes to it a designation, one name. Also, a wooden building that has several attributes within it has them. Also, you will find further that this holy wall, which was built, was in parts; each and every stone was separate from the clods of earth, by itself, and the lime by itself, etc. And after the builder came and joined all these parts with his wisdom, this within that, and this beside that, and they became one wall, etc., thus, then, all is one piece and one part. And so is the matter with us, etc." And there, on folios 25 and 29, he compares it to the human body, joined of bones and sinews and flesh, head and eye and ear and nose and mouth and hands and feet, and the whole is called by the name man, Reuben or Simeon. And on folios 25, 26 and 27 he wrote: "The sum of the matter is that the First Cause, which is called Ein Sof by all the Kabbalists, is He who emanated, created, formed and made, and He is hidden within Ze'ir Anpin, and then Ze'ir Anpin is the one who rules over all creatures, leads them, feeds them and sustains them, by the power of Ein Sof within him. Therefore He is our God, and we are His people, for our souls are His portion, and Him we shall worship, and He is the God of our fathers, in whose hand is the conduct of the worlds, for reward and punishment. But Ein Sof, with the other partzufim above Ze'ir and his Nukva, if human beings order their prayers to them individually, without praying to Ze'ir Anpin, even if they direct their intention to the soul hidden in them, they will cry out and not be answered. And on the contrary, those who pray to them will be punished, for it is the will of the First Cause that He be the one who brings out and brings in His flow to the lower beings, and there is no other besides Him. See there carefully." And the words of the Rabbi, the author of Kisse Eliyahu, stand against the words of the Rambam, of blessed memory, in his commentary on the Mishnah, in his composition, and in Moreh Nevukhim, and against the words of the pious one, the author of Chovot ha-Levavot, in the Gate of Unity, and Rabbi Saadia Gaon in the book Emunot ve-De'ot, and the Roke'ach, who wrote that His oneness, may He be blessed, is not like the one of a pair, nor like the one of a species, nor like the one man who is divided into many ones. And not one like a simple body, etc., which receives division without end. But the Name, may He be blessed, is one with a oneness that has no like. Also, Kisse Eliyahu wrote that Ein Sof is the soul of Atik, and Arikh Anpin, and Abba and Imma, and Ze'ir and his Nukva, and my teachers, of blessed memory, the aforesaid, wrote that He is not a body, nor a force in a body! And according to his words He is a force in a body. Also he wrote that Arikh Anpin, Abba and Imma preceded Ze'ir Anpin who is our God (according to his words), and he is called a son of Abba and Imma, etc. And our Rabbis of blessed memory said that He is eternal before all that exists, and that every existent other than Him is not eternal, etc. Also he wrote concerning Ein Sof, blessed be He, that no worship pertains to Him, and no invocation at all. And no name applies to Him: not YHVH, nor Adonai, etc. but only to Ze'ir Anpin and his Nukva in the World of Emanation alone, and not to Arikh Anpin, Abba and Imma, and Ze'ir and his Nukva that are in the emanated worlds above the World of Emanation, as explained there, 4, 49, the end of side a, and on folio 53....

Grammar
  • The paragraph is the questioner's reply. The respondent's words and Kisse Eliyahu are quoted in double marks; a verse inside them is in single marks.
  • ולא הבנתי דעתך וכוונתך בזה, אם זה ... או היפך דבריו: an indirect question, 'whether ... or ...', with אם introducing the first alternative.
  • אדרבא שם: 'on the contrary' reverses what was expected; the book says the opposite of what the questioner sought.
  • Indirect reports introduced by כתב ש- or כתבו ש- (for example 'Also he wrote that ...') carry no quotation marks; only the direct formula כתב: opens a quotation.
  • ואין עוד מלבדו is an embedded verse (Deut 4:35, 4:39), translated from its Hebrew as 'there is no other besides Him'.

The questioner's second letter (חזר השואל והשיב). The Wikisource text ends mid-sentence ('....') and the English keeps the break.

Apparatus
  • Prov 1:5 (2:4.22–25): 'ישמע חכם ויוסף לקח', rendered as the verse's future.
  • Deut 4:35 and 4:39 (2:4.292–294): 'ואין עוד מלבדו'.
  • שם (2:4.61) is read as 'there', the place in the book; the other sense, 'the name', does not fit the sentence.
  • The author writes ארוך (2:4.365) and שאריך (2:4.387) for Arikh; both are rendered Arikh Anpin.
  • ד׳ (2:4.460) is read as 4, the folio; the numeral is kept because the author writes דף in full nearby.
  • Deut 6:13: 'ואתו תעבד', 'and Him you shall worship', is echoed in ואותו נעבוד (2:4.236-237), with the verb in the first person plural.
2:5

And how can we leave all the divinities that are above the World of Emanation, and worship specifically Ze'ir and his Nukva, who are in the World of Emanation, since there have already preceded him several Atikin and Arikhei Anpin, and Abba and Imma, and Ze'ir and his Nukva in the upper worlds; there is no number of those still closer to Ein Sof?

and-how shall-we-leave all the-divinities that above the-World of-Emanation and-worship specifically Ze'ir and-his-Nukva who-are-in-the World-of-Emanation who-already preceded him several Atikin and-Arikhei Anpin and-Abba-and-Imma and-Ze'ir and-his-Nukva in-the-worlds upper without number the-close-ones to-Ein Sof more

Grammar
  • נניח and ונעבוד are first-person plural imperfects (not cohortatives, which would end in ה) in a rhetorical question: 'how shall we leave ... and worship'; the English reads 'can we leave'.
  • קדמו לו כמה עתיקין: the verb comes before its subject (verb-subject order), and לו means 'before him'.
  • The last clause, אין מספר הקרובים לאין סוף יותר?, means 'there is no number of those still closer to Ein Sof?': יותר is the comparative of הקרובים ('closer'), not 'and more'. The question mark is the Hebrew's.

The questioner's letter, in his voice. Ze'ir and his Nukva are named as the partzufim the question asks us to worship.

Apparatus
  • Wikisource base text; not yet collated with the 1931 scan (decisions, Q2).
  • ואו"א is one abbreviated word for Abba and Imma.
2:6

And our early rabbis said that it is not fitting to worship, to give thanks, to magnify, and to glorify, except to the first God of all that exists apart from Him! And why should we leave the principal Ein Sof, that contracts above all of them, with all the partzufim close to it, and worship that which is very far from it, which is the last partzuf of the World of Emanation? All this, make us understand, our lord, let us go and pursue the LORD our Maker the Creator of the beginning. And do not pour upon us a word of Belial, God forbid. For who has gathered grace and good understanding in his palms, to have insight and to know the LORD through investigating divine matters in the principles of the faith, like you. Who will ascend to the mountain of the LORD, and who will stand in His holy place, like you, for I am more brutish than any man, and I have no understanding of a man. And the Rock knows the secrets of the heart, the examiner of hearts, for I did not give sleep to my eyes, and my sleep was taken from my eyes until I find solutions and whoever comes to purify himself, they help him, to provide for him a guide to the way of holiness by intellect and knowledge, like Khalkhal and Darda, and among the sages of truth a sage and an artisan, like Ethan and Heman, for perhaps the rabbis who lack this wisdom are to us false oracles and misleading ones, God forbid. And you, my lord, to you its secrets are revealed, and your treasure will fill the bellies of your disciples, they will be sated and delight in your goodness, and upon us to pay the wages of your work. And you, do not withhold good from its owners. And here I adjure you by the God of heaven: make Your face shine upon us, to answer the weary with a word spoken in its proper setting, and we shall be servants to my lord. And our lips will ask a great reward for your goodness, then we shall not be ashamed, neither in this world nor in the world to come, and we shall return and graze among the lilies from the company of sages and discerning ones.

Grammar
  • אמרו שאין ראוי is indirect speech ('said that it is not fitting'), so the segment has no quotation marks; the four infinitives that follow are its objects.
  • ולמה נניח ... ונעבוד ...? is a rhetorical question in first-person plural imperfects (not cohortatives: no ה ending); the Hebrew closes it with '?'.
  • מי יעלה בהר ה' and כי בער אנכי מאיש are embedded verses (Ps 24:3; Prov 30:2) with no quotation marks; their imperfects keep the verses' future sense.
  • הביננו אדונינו נלכה נרדפה: an imperative with a vocative ('our lord'), then a true cohortative pair ('let us go and pursue', after Hos 6:3).
  • ישבע ויתענגו are imperfects after תמלא and read as a result: 'they will be sated and delight'.
  • המצטמצם is a hitpael present participle ('that contracts'), and השכל וידוע is the infinitive pair of Jer 9:23 ('to have insight and to know').

The questioner's letter, in his voice, addressed to the respondent as 'my lord'. Biblical phrases are embedded and unmarked.

Apparatus
  • Ps 24:3 (embedded): מי יעלה בהר ה' ומי יקום במקום קדשו.
  • Prov 30:2 (embedded): כי בער אנכי מאיש ולא בינת אדם לי.
  • Ps 44:22 (embedded): יודע תעלומות לב. Prov 17:3: ובֹחֵן לִבּוֹת, 'examiner of hearts'.
  • Ps 17:14 (embedded): וצפונך תמלא בטנם.
  • Prov 3:27: אל תמנע טוב מבעליו.
  • Ps 80:4 (Hebrew numbering, embedded): האר פניך.
  • Isa 50:4 (embedded): לעות את יעף דבר.
  • Prov 25:11 (embedded): דבר דבור על אופניו; the source writes אפניו.
  • Song 2:16 (embedded): הָרֹעֶה בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים.
  • 1 Kings 5:11 (Hebrew): the wise men Ethan, Heman, Khalkhal and Darda.
  • Hos 6:3 (allusion): נרדפה לדעת את ה'; the author writes נלכה נרדפה את ה'.
  • Ps 41:9 (allusion): דבר בליעל יצוק בו; the author writes ואל תצוק בנו דבר בליעל.
  • Prov 30:4 (allusion): מי אסף רוח בחפניו; and Prov 3:4: חן ושכל טוב.
  • Jer 9:23 (allusion): השכל וידע אותי; the author writes השכל וידוע את ה'.
  • Ps 132:4–5 (allusion): אם אתן שנת לעיני ... עד אמצא; the author writes עד אמצא פתרונים.
  • Isa 35:8 (allusion): ודרך הקדש.
  • Lam 2:14 (allusion): משאות שוא ומדוחים.
  • Gen 24:3 (allusion): ואשביעך ביהוה אלהי השמים; the author writes משביעך באלהי השמים.

2:7

Second Reply. I saw all that is written in the letter of the eminent one, a tree whose branches are many, its height like the height of cedars, After the pardon for the delay, for the pressure of the times is outstretched, and every delay is for good. When I looked at the letter, behold, you opened your mouth, by mentioning divinities, thinking that it is against us. And what are we, that you murmur against us, and your scorn does not reach us, but only to the sages of Israel, whose least is thicker than your loins, and all Israel rests on them, and by their merit the world stands. Woe to you, for you have brought out against them words that are not according to the law, in innocence, and in its place guile. But your judgment has already been made clear, by the mouth of all the masters of wisdom. And as for what you wrote about Kisse Eliyahu, that on folio 3 he likens His oneness, may He be blessed, to the other unities. You are already walking in darkness. Surely the beginning of his words on folio 20 is that all these likenesses are about holy lights, which have no grasp, no form and no likeness, neither in intellect nor in knowledge at all and in principle, but so that the intellect can receive them, we were permitted to liken. And on folio 4b he wrote that all the epithets and attributes are in the manner of likeness, in the sefirot and the holy lights, the emanated beings. But in Him, may He be blessed, there is not in Him any likeness and form, and grasp in thought at all and in principle. And as for what you wrote, how can we leave the other partzufim and worship Ze'ir Anpin with the power in him, Ein Sof, blessed be He. The Master, Kisse Eliyahu, has already explained on folio 25b, that when we call upon Ze'ir Anpin, we call all the partzufim together, with a soul hidden in them. And as for what you wrote, why do we leave the partzufim closest to Ein Sof and call upon Ze'ir Anpin. Because it is known that among the inner attributes some are judgment and some are mercy, and this one includes them all, and therefore the Emanator wanted to perform His actions through this vessel. Before you object to the likenesses concerning the upper ones, which you have no right to ponder, all the more so to mock, object to your corporeal hand, which does all the labors, and the head above does not do anything. Also, the power of speech, which is your glory, above every living creature, why was it not given above your eyes. But thus His wisdom decreed, may He be blessed. And if you have proper counsel, go to your Creator and counsel Him. And as for what you wrote, that the words of Kisse Eliyahu are against the Rambam, etc., who wrote that it is not a force in a body, and according to the words of Kisse Eliyahu it is a force in a body. Surely all the Kabbalists with one mouth answer and say that whoever ascribes corporeality to the sefirot, like you, is a denier and has no share in the God of Israel. And as for their having called them subtle lights, it is only to soothe the ear! We have to ask about what the Rambam wrote: "Let him direct his heart toward the Shekhinah and pray." And in the Guide he wrote that the Shekhinah is a created light. And more than this, what he wrote about the glory of the LORD, that it is created. If so, how did Israel go out to the opening of their tents and bow down to the created thing. And more than this, what he wrote, that every form which the prophets saw and spoke with is a created light. If so, we have no prophecy through the Creator, but all of it from the side of the created ones. And if it is said that the created thing was attached to the Creator, then, in your opinion, it is a force in a body! Your answer will quickly spring up, the end of the verse: "They refuse to know Me, says the LORD."

Grammar
  • תשובה שנית is a heading ('Second Reply'): Chapter 2 is a correspondence, and the writer now answers the questioner in the second person (פערת פיך, כנגדינו).
  • אילן שענפיו מרובים, רומו כגובה ארזים is an image in apposition to כתב האלוף. Its last phrase alludes to Amos 2:9 and is unmarked.
  • Each 'ומה שכתבת' clause answers one point of the questioner's letter, in the order he gave them.
  • שכתב הרמב"ם: יכוין לבו כנגד השכינה ויתפלל is an explicit quotation with the formula 'wrote', so it takes double quotation marks; the Hebrew colon is kept.
  • ותשובתך מהרה תצמח alludes to Isa 58:8 and takes no marks. ס' מאנו דעת אותי נאם ה' is a quoted verse with the abbreviation ס' before it, so it takes quotation marks.

The respondent's reply, in his voice. The Kabbalistic terms and the book's abbreviations follow the decisions for the work.

Other readings (1)
  • ותיעצנו: and counsel us suffix -נו as 'us' the same spelling read with the plural suffix: go to your Creator and then give us counsel.

  • Isa 58:8 (allusion): ארכתך מהרה תצמח.
  • Amos 2:9 (allusion): אשר גבהו כגובה ארזים.
  • Folio numbers (3, 20, 4b, 25b) are the author's own; no reference is added.
  • Exod 16:7 (allusion): ונחנו מה כי תלונו עלינו; the base text prints תלינו, and the English follows the verse.
  • 1 Kings 12:10 (allusion; also 2 Chr 10:10): קטני עבה ממתני אבי; the author writes קטנם עבה ממתניך.
  • Isa 50:10 (allusion): אשר הלך חשכים.
  • Exod 33:10 (allusion): ויקומו ... איש פתח אהלו והשתחוו.
  • 2:7.141: the base text prints ואודות; the English reads ואורות (cf. אורות קדושים, 2:7.108).
  • 2:7.397: ס' not expanded in the text; read as סוף (end of the verse); ספר or סימן are the alternatives.

2:8

Reply from the questioner. My soul longed to hear words refined like cast mirrors, from the heights of heaven, burning. For I am poor in all knowledge, longing for the shade of the gourd. And instead of your humility making me great, you gave me to drink many waters, bitter as gall. You made me like a booth in a cucumber field, and my soul is incurable by praises of deceit (like the blessing of the wicked Balaam), dreadful ones. And with the words of a slanderer you concluded, and you resembled a man who casts off discipline, and a bereaved bear. And in truth this is not the way of the Torah. Our holy Torah, its ways are ways of pleasantness. And you shall love your neighbor as yourself. "What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow." Thus said Hillel, Prince of Israel! He stated the sum of the matter: as for my having opened my mouth to disparage the sages of Israel, and having brought out against them words that are not according to the law. Far be it from me to disparage any person, even a gentile, all the more so an Israelite. And I know no place in my words for what you claim, that there is disparagement in them. And if one raises difficulties against them from the words of our Rabbis of blessed memory, and reveals a place of contradiction, there is no prohibition in this at all. And also in the Talmud they raise difficulties even against those greater than they, and bring proof to refute their words, and say, "Refutation of Rabbi So-and-so." That of Rabbi So-and-so is a fabrication (the Arukh's reading: berota), and in Sanhedrin and in Berakhot we say: "The one who sees the rainbow must bow down, for it is written: 'Like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud, etc., and I saw and fell on my face.'" "They curse it in the West, etc. Rabbi Abahu blasphemes against it, etc." And behold, in this your letter I found a complaint; a reply I did not find. Is it I who called these partzufim divinities? Did not the Kabbalists themselves say so. Go and learn from the intention of the blessings and the prayer: who is our God, and who is the God of our fathers. And in the Zohar he asks: "Who is this Elohim, such and such?" Moreover, for the Kabbalists explained that many worlds, thousands of thousands and myriads of myriads, were emanated, created, formed and made, only they did not put forth a hand to explain them because of their great concealment. For they are very subtle lights. And each world is comprised of ten sefirot. And each sefirah is comprised of ten details of details, as we said in the World of Emanation. And all of them are in the aspect of circles, this within this, and this inside that. And likewise in the aspect of the sefirot of straightness, which are in the form of a man of upright stature with 248 limbs, etc. All these worlds, each one of them comprises two aspects, of circles and of straightness, in general and in particular. And all the words of the Kabbalists and their explanations are only in the World of Emanation, which has already been coarsened and revealed more; and in it they explained all the matters of the comprehensive partzufim, which are five: Arikh Anpin, and Abba, and Imma, and Ze'ir, and his Nukva. Since it has already been made clear to you from their words that they say the partzufim were coarsened and revealed, and that they call the aforementioned partzufim divinities, when they say our God and the God of our fathers in prayer and in blessings, and that they intend a known attribute in every word. Your complaint does not stand against me, neither as a charge of corporeality nor as a charge of divinity, but against them, for they said it, and they said it. And the difficulty returns to its place: how shall we leave aside Ein Sof together with all the sefirot that are in the upper worlds, together with Arikh Anpin and Abba and Imma, and worship Ze'ir Anpin and say that He is our God, and we are His people and His servants; He made us, and to Him we are. In this letter of yours (where you said, "since it is known that the inner attributes are, some of them judgment and some of them mercy, etc.") you have already made a complete admission that this is your opinion: that no worship and no prayer applies to the Cause over all the causes, but only to Ze'ir Anpin, as the Rav Mikdash Melekh wrote, and Kisse Eliyahu, and Mahari Lopes in the Gate of the True Faith. Therefore we need you to resolve and answer for us how this opinion of the Kabbalists, that all our worship and our prayers are to Ze'ir Anpin and his soul, will agree with our holy Torah, the Written Torah and the Oral Torah. And as for your anger that burned against me, and your saying that I ascribe corporeality to the sefirot, I also know no place for this in my words, for I said nothing that I did not find in their books. They said that the World of Emanation has in it a body, a soul and a garment. And it is not hidden from you that light, air and fire are subtle and light bodies. Moreover, they themselves explained their words, and said that the upper worlds and the partzufim above Arikh Anpin they did not speak of, only from Arikh Anpin and downward, since they had already been coarsened and revealed more. Behold, it is plain to you from their words that the sefirot they speak of were coarsened and revealed more than those above them, and they themselves admit that the sefirot they speak of were coarsened.

Grammar
  • The paragraph is the questioner's reply in chapter 2 (תשובה מהשואל): 'I' is the questioner and 'you' is the respondent, who is addressed throughout.
  • In 'איותה נפשי לשמוע', the soul is the subject of the verb of longing and the infinitive is its object; 'מוזקקות' and 'מוצקות' agree with 'אמרות' (words).
  • 'ובדברי נרגן סיימת ... דמית': the verbs have no object written. 'דמית' with ל is read as qal, 'you resembled' (Ezek 31:2); read as piel it would be 'you likened (me)'. 'פרוע מוסר' is one phrase, 'one who casts off discipline' (Prov 13:18).
  • Aramaic (Bavli): 'מה דעלך סני לחברך' is Hillel's saying; 'הא דר' פלוני בדותא היא' and 'לייטי עלה במערבא ... מגדף בה' ('they curse it in the West ... he blasphemes against it') are Talmudic Aramaic. 'מאן אלהים דא כך וכך' is Zohar Aramaic. 'אמרינן' ('we say') introduces the Talmudic statement.
  • 'ריש מלין אמר' is Aramaic and echoes Dan 7:1 (ראש מלין אמר): 'he stated the sum of the matter'. What follows, 'מה שאני פערתי פי ...', restates the respondent's charge of 2:7.
  • 'איך נניח האין סוף ... ונעבוד לז"א ונאמר' is one question: הניח is 'leave aside', and ונעבוד ונאמר are the second and third verbs under the same 'how' ('how shall we leave Ein Sof aside, and worship Ze'ir Anpin and say ...').

A letter in the correspondence of chapter 2. The questioner answers the respondent's charge that he disparaged the sages and the Kabbalists; the English keeps the questioner's voice and the respondent's 'you'.

Other readings (3)
  • ולאיש פרוע מוסר ודוב שכול דמית: and you likened me to a man who casts off discipline, and to a bereaved bear piel of דמה Reads דמית as piel, 'you likened', with an object (me) understood; the Hebrew writes none.
  • דחלות: fearful (the soul afraid) translator Reads דחלות as describing the soul, not the praises; an Aramaic word for 'idols' (דחלא) is a further possibility that the context does not support.
  • ענותך תרבני: your answering would increase me ענות as 'answering' Reads ענותך as 'your answering'; the allusion to Ps 18:36 (ענותך תרבני) favours 'your humility'.
Apparatus
  • The unit has no marked Wikisource additions; the 1931 scan has not been collated (decisions, Q2).
  • Job 37:18 (embedded allusion): 'like cast mirrors' (כראי מוצקות), from 'like a cast mirror'. Ps 12:7 (echo): 'refined' (מוזקקות) of words.
  • Job 7:2 (embedded): 'longing for the shade' (שואף לצל). Jonah 4:6 (allusion): 'the gourd' (הקיקיון).
  • Ps 18:36 (embedded): 'ענותך תרבני', 'your humility has made me great', turned to irony.
  • Isa 1:8 (embedded): the verse reads 'like a hut in a vineyard, like a lodge in a cucumber field' (כסוכה בכרם כמלונה במקשה). The author takes the second clause (כמלונה במקשה) alone.
  • Hos 13:8 and Prov 17:12 (embedded): 'a bereaved bear' (דוב שכול). Prov 13:18 (embedded): 'one who casts off discipline' (פורע מוסר). Prov 18:8 (embedded): 'the words of a slanderer' (דברי נרגן).
  • Prov 3:17 (embedded): 'its ways are ways of pleasantness' (דרכיה דרכי נועם; the verse reads 'דרכיה דרכי נעם').
  • Lev 19:18: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself' (ואהבת לרעך כמוך).
  • Dan 7:1 (echo): 'ריש מלין אמר', from 'ראש מלין אמר', 'he told the sum of the matters'. Esth 4:16 (echo): 'not according to the law' (אשר לא כדת).
  • Ezek 1:28 (quoted in part): 'like the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud' and 'I saw and fell on my face' (ואראה ואפול על פני).
  • Ps 100:3 (embedded): 'He made us, and to Him we are' (הוא עשנו ולו אנחנו). The verse's ketiv is 'ולא אנחנו' and its qere 'ולו אנחנו'; the author writes the qere. 'His people and His servants' (עמו ועבדיו) replaces the verse's 'and the flock of His pasture'; the English follows the author's wording.
  • The saying 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow' is attributed to Hillel by the author, who gives no reference.
  • בדותא / ברותא: the printed text reads בדותא ('fabrication'); the note in parentheses gives the Arukh's reading ברותא, which the English leaves transliterated (berota).
  • מא"א (2:8.521) is read as מאריך אנפין, from the same sentence ('שלמעלה מאריך אנפין ... רק מא"א ולמטה'); the reading is certain.
  • דחלות (2:8.41): read as 'dreadful ones', agreeing with תהלות; the alternative, 'fearful' (the soul afraid), is in `readings`.
2:9

Would that, my lord, you would inform me also, who governs all the hidden worlds, of which the Kabbalists did not speak, and who feeds and sustains them. Whether Ze'ir Anpin, this one in Emanation, is the one who feeds and sustains them, and to him they worship and bow down, or Ein Sof is their God, and to Him alone they worship; and we worship Ze'ir Anpin, for he feeds us, and he is our God, as the Kabbalists said. It follows from this that Ein Sof is the God of the upper ones and Ze'ir Anpin the God of the lower ones, and here we have two authorities, God forbid. And explicitly, some of them said: "all the great work of the LORD," by implication there is a small one. And our true Rabbis said, as cited in Menorat ha-Maor, chapter 143, that at the time of the giving of the Torah He tore open for them seven heavens and opened seven lands, and said to them, to Israel: "Understand the upper ones and understand the lower ones, and know that there is no God besides Me, neither among the upper ones nor among the lower ones: I am the LORD your God." And in Midrash Rabbah, Parashat Yitro, they said: "I am the LORD your God." Rabbi Abbahu said: "A parable of a king of flesh and blood who reigns; he has a father, or a brother, or a son. The Holy One, blessed be He, said: I am not so. I am the first and I am the last, and besides Me there is no God. I am the first, for I have no father. I am the last, for I have no son. And besides Me there is no God, for I have no brother." Thus far the wording of the Midrash, etc. The Rabbi Etz Yosef, of blessed memory, that is to say, "that a king of flesh and blood, his kingship is not complete, because he has a father, whom he must honor, and who shares the kingship with him, or he has a brother who has a share in the honor of kingship, or he has a son who exercises authority with him, and after him is heir to the throne. And the explanation: He has no father, for He is the First Cause. And He has no brother, for He is one, and has no second. And He has no son, in that the effects were not drawn from Him by nature, as a son is drawn from a father, as some thought (this is the view of the Kabbalists, who said that Ze'ir Anpin is a son of Abba and Imma, and he is a father to the effects that follow him, etc., and he has a sister or sisters, his nukvin) for according to that view he has no power to change any of the things, and his kingship is not complete. But the Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'I am the LORD your God,' for this is His power to bring them out of the land of Egypt, since His kingship is complete and there is none who can stay His hand." Thus far his words.

Grammar
  • אחלי (2:9.1) is a wish, 'would that'. The paragraph is the questioner's letter, addressed to 'my lord' (2:9.2), and is kept in his voice.
  • The sentence 'אם ... או' (2:9.18, 2:9.30) gives two alternatives, 'whether ... or', in one statement that ends with a period, not a question; each alternative has its own verbs (עובדים, ומשתחוים; לבדו עובדים).
  • ונמצא לפי זה (2:9.50-52) is the questioner's conclusion from the two alternatives, and הרי כאן שתי רשויות ח"ו (2:9.62-66) is his objection to it.
  • From ובהדיא אמרו (2:9.67) the paragraph quotes its sources: the Menorat ha-Maor, the Midrash Rabbah with its parable, and the commentary Etz Yosef. Each quotation is in quotation marks; the Etz Yosef passage runs from ר"ל (2:9.171) to the closing עכ"ל (2:9.289).
  • Aramaic: נוקבין דיליה (2:9.254-255) and ולית דימחי בידיה (2:9.286-288); the English gives the sense of each.

The questioner's letter in his voice (chapter 2 correspondence). The English keeps each sentence and the quotation boundaries. Names and terms are transliterated per the decisions. 'God' is used throughout for the God of Israel, including where the questioner puts it in the Kabbalists' mouth ('our God', 'the God of the upper ones'), as the case ruling requires; lower-case 'god' is not used, since the Hebrew does not mark foreignness or plurality here.

Apparatus
  • Base text: Wikisource, not yet collated against the 1931 scan (Q2).
  • Deut 11:7: 'all the great work of the LORD' renders the words the author quotes, את כל מעשה ה' הגדול; the verse continues 'which He did', which the author does not quote. The inference מכלל דאיכא קטן turns on 'the great'.
  • Exod 20:2: 'I am the LORD your God' (אנכי ה' אלהיך), quoted in the Menorat ha-Maor passage, the Midrash, and the Etz Yosef passage.
  • Isa 44:6: the Midrash's אני ראשון ... ומבלעדי אין אלהים echoes Isa 44:6; the English keeps the author's wording, 'I am first ... and besides Me there is no God'.
  • The reference 'פ' קמ"ג' to Menorat ha-Maor is kept as written and has not been checked.
  • Dan 4:32 (Aramaic): ולית דימחי בידיה echoes ולא איתי די ימחא בידה, 'and there is none who can stay His hand'.
  • באצילות is 'in Emanation' (the word is אצילות without עולם); the four worlds are Emanation, Creation, Formation, Making.
2:10

In the Yerushalmi, Shabbat, chapter Bemah Ishah, our Sages of blessed memory said: "'And the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.' Rabbi Reuven said: At that hour an angel came down and slapped that wicked one on his mouth, and said to him: 'Is your word right, and is there a son for him?' He returned and said: 'Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meishach and Abed-nego, who sent His angel and saved His servants.' 'His son' is not written here, but 'His angel.' Thus far." That is to say, Nebuchadnezzar the wicked thought that the angels are effects, descending in a chain of descent from him by nature, like a son from the father, according to the words of the Kabbalists concerning the sefirot of all the worlds, and likewise the souls; and for this the angel slapped him. And he returned and said: 'who sent His angel, etc.' Here you have it explicit, coming out of the words of Midrash Rabbah and the Yerushalmi, contrary to the words of the Kabbalists. And all that exists, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought into being in His kindness, something from nothing, from the first form down to a small gnat; and not that they are drawn from His essence, as the son comes into being by the power of the seed drawn from his father.

Grammar
  • The Yerushalmi is quoted as the author's source, and its Aramaic is translated as he gives it. Dan 3:25 and 3:28 are quoted inside it, in single quotation marks.
  • 'ע"כ' (2:10.53) closes the Yerushalmi quotation. From 2:10.54 the author argues in his own voice, and his argument turns on the words 'בר' (son) and 'מלאכיה' (his angel).
  • 'ובר אית ליה?' is an Aramaic question, 'and is there a son for him?'. 'סטרו' (2:10.21, 2:10.76) is a verb of the angel's action, 'slapped him'.
  • 'ולא שהם נמשכים' (2:10.107-109) is 'and not that they are drawn': the negative ולא rejects the Kabbalists' claim that the angels and all things are drawn from His essence like a son from the seed. 'ושכל' (2:10.95) opens with ש, 'that'.

The Yerushalmi passage is the author's source. The argument of the paragraph is set by 2:10.54 onward, where the author draws his conclusion from it against the Kabbalists.

Ancient Near East
  • Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had Shadrach, Meishach and Abed-nego thrown into a furnace (Dan 3), and called the fourth figure he saw there 'like a son of the gods' (Dan 3:25). In the Yerushalmi's story an angel strikes him for it. The author quotes it against the Kabbalists' claim that the angels descend from God as a son from a father.
Apparatus
  • Dan 3:25 (Aramaic): the Yerushalmi's wording 'וריויה די רביעאה דמי לבר אלהין' is kept; 'son of the gods' is the verse's phrase.
  • Dan 3:28 (Aramaic): the blessing of the three men, with 'בריה' contrasted with 'מלאכיה' as the Yerushalmi gives them.
  • Yerushalmi: tractate and chapter as the author gives them (Shabbat, 'Bemah Ishah'); no folio or halakhah number is added.
  • Q2 (Wikisource additions): the base text is translated; no word is flagged until the 1931 scan is collated.
2:11

The conclusion from all this is that no face or form is to be worshipped of all the created things that exist in the upper and the lower world, which the Name, may He be blessed, brought into being in His kindness. For to Him alone it is fitting to worship and to pray, and for this the commandment and the warning came at Sinai: "I am the LORD your God. You shall have no other gods," as the Rambam of blessed memory wrote in chapter two of the Laws of Idolatry. And in chapter three of the Laws of Repentance he wrote, and these are his words: "And these are those who have no share in the world to come, but are cut off and perish for the greatness of their wickedness and their sins, forever and ever: the heretics and the apikorsim, etc." And in the law that follows it he wrote: "Five are those that are called heretics. The one who says that there is no God, and no ruler of the world, and the one who says that there is a ruler, but they are two or more, and the one who says that there is one Lord, but He is a body and possessed of a form, and the one who says that He is not alone the first and the rock of all. Likewise one who worships one other than Him in order to be an intercessor between him and the Lord of the worlds. Each of these five is a heretic. Thus far." And the Rav Lechem Mishneh wrote on the fourth division that our Master wrote, "and the one who says that He is not alone the first, etc." The Ravad wrote: "like one who said, your God is a great painter, but He found for Himself great pigments, formlessness and void, and darkness and water and wind, and with them made what He made." Thus far, the words of the Ravad. And the Rav Lechem Mishneh explains that his intention is to add to the words of our Master that although he concedes that no cause preceded our God, for whose sake He came to be, but says that He created the world something from something, then this one is a heretic; see there. In our case, the belief of the new Kabbalah, as explained in their books, according to our understanding and the understanding of many great ones, wise of heart, among our Rabbis who separated from it, early and late, like the Ribash and Chavot Yair, cited in Pitchei Teshuvah and the other later authorities: in it have gathered and come three or four of these words that our Rabbis said, that whoever believes thus has no share in the world to come. First, a multiplicity of divinities: Ein Sof, and Adam Kadma'ah, and Adam Kadmon, and Atik, and Arikh Anpin, and Abba and Imma, and Ze'ir and his Nukva! Second, that they have a subtle body, namely light, and Ein Sof is a soul to these bodies. Third, that the worship is not to the First Cause, which they call Ein Sof, but to Ze'ir Anpin, which is the last cause among these causes. Fourth, that he is an intermediary drawing down the flow from those upper attributes, which are Atik, Arikh Anpin, Abba and Imma, and they call him son of Abba and Imma, and he is also father to the Keter of Creation, according to the chain of descent of the worlds, in their opinion, the Merciful One save us.

Grammar
  • The Rambam's words run from 2:11.51 ('וז"ל') to 2:11.125 ('ע"כ'). They are cut short at 'וכו'' (2:11.70); 'ובדין שאחריו כ'' (2:11.71-73) is the author's link, so the quotation marks close and open again around it. The author's gloss starts at 2:11.126.
  • 'כ'' (2:11.73, 2:11.140) is 'wrote', an abbreviation of כתב; 'שכ'' (2:11.39) is 'that wrote'. 'הרב' (2:11.127, 2:11.165) is a word of the text, 'the Rav', before the book's name.
  • 'שאין לעבוד' (2:11.4-5) is 'that one must not worship': 'לעבוד' is the verb 'to worship', used of God throughout the paragraph.
  • 'שם' in 'שאין שם אלוה' (2:11.79-81), 'שיש שם מנהיג' (2:11.86-88) and 'שיש שם רבון' (2:11.95-97) is the adverb 'there' of the existential 'there is', not 'name'.
  • In the long sentence at 2:11.191-232 the subject of 'נקבצו באו' (2:11.218-219) is 'תלת וארבע מלי' (2:11.221-223), 'three or four words'; 'בה' is 'in it', the belief of the new Kabbalah. The words between ('כפי המבואר … ושאר אחרונים') say by whose understanding. 'דאמור רבנן' is Aramaic: 'that the Rabbis said'.
  • 'חדא', 'שנית', 'שלישית', 'רביעית' (2:11.233, 248, 259, 275) number the four 'words'. The first is a noun phrase (רבוי האלוהות); the others open with שהם, שהעבודה, שהוא.

The paragraph is the author's conclusion from the Rambam's law (the Rambam, the Lechem Mishneh and the Ravad are quoted), followed by the four 'words' of the Rabbis that he finds in the new Kabbalah.

Other readings (1)
  • נקבצו באו בה תלת וארבע מלי מהני דאמור רבנן דהמאמין כן אין לו חלק לעה"ב: the authorities gathered and came against it: three or four of these words that our Rabbis said, "Whoever believes thus has no share in the world to come." alternative subject The reading of the draft, which makes the Ribash, Chavot Yair and the later authorities the subject and בה 'against it'; the English chosen takes 'three or four words' as the subject and בה as 'in it'.
Ancient Near East
  • The Mishneh Torah is the Rambam's code of Jewish law; the Laws of Idolatry and the Laws of Repentance are two of its sections, as cited here.
  • The Lechem Mishneh is a commentary on the Mishneh Torah. Pitchei Teshuvah is a commentary on the Shulchan Arukh.
Apparatus
  • Exod 20:2-3: the author quotes 'אנכי ה' אלהיך לא יהיה לך אלהים אחרים', leaving out 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt …' (v. 2) and 'על פני' (v. 3); the English follows his wording, without 'before Me'.
  • Rambam, Laws of Idolatry ch. 2 and Laws of Repentance ch. 3 (Mishneh Torah), as the author gives them; no halakhah number is added. The Rambam's quotation is cut short at 'וכו'' (2:11.70).
  • Gen 1:2: 'תהו ובהו וחשך ומים ורוח' in the Ravad's words echoes the verse ('formless and void, and darkness … and the wind (or spirit) of God … the waters'); here the words are the painter's materials, so 'formlessness and void' and 'wind'.
  • The Lechem Mishneh and the Ravad are quoted as the author gives them; 'וכו'' is kept as 'etc.'.
  • יש מיש: 'something from something', translated, not transliterated (decisions, wave 1: יש מאין / יש מיש).
  • חו"י: the expansion Chavot Yair (the fixed spelling in the decisions) is a reading, not a certainty.
  • שם (2:11.80, 87, 96) is 'there'; 'name' is not possible in the grammar of 'שיש שם'.
2:12

And this I have seen in your reply. And I will tell these words that split roofs, since you replied to my words that I said to you: how shall we set aside Ein Sof and the rest of the partzufim close to Ein Sof and worship Ze'ir Anpin? And your reply was, because the other attributes are some judgment and some mercy, and this one is composed of them all. And for this reason the Emanator wished to perform His actions through this vessel, etc. And you brought me an analogy from the bodily hand, which does all the tasks, while the head, which is above, does nothing. Also the power of speech, which is splendor, etc.; all these words of yours are nothing but astonishing words! I asked you about their saying that Ze'ir Anpin is our God, and we worship him, and you answer me from those who act upon us by the will of their Maker. Do we then worship all those who act upon us by the will of their Maker? And shall we say that they are our God? Surely the sun acts for us in many good actions: to shine for us, to warm the air and the earth, to make grass sprout, and to ripen the fruit. Shall we worship her? The moon and the stars too act upon the lower beings by the will of the Creator, may He be blessed, as it is said: "and from the precious things of the yield of the sun, and from the precious things of the growth of the moons." Shall we worship them? The earth, the water and the fire also act to sprout grass and trees and to raise them. And with fire we do all that we want: to bake and to cook all our food. And in most crafts one blows on a charcoal fire and brings out a tool for its work. Shall we worship one of them? And His will, may He be blessed, to perform His actions through intermediary agents is plain and clear in the verses. "Let the waters swarm, let the earth bring forth a living creature, let the earth sprout grass," and it is said: "He makes His messengers winds, His ministers a blazing fire," and more and more, in every case of one doing its errand. And yet, despite all this, the Name, may He be blessed, commanded us to worship Him alone, and warned us not to worship any one besides Him. And at the chosen assembly, when He revealed Himself on Mount Sinai, He gave His voice before His host: "I am the LORD your God … You shall have no other gods before Me." And it is said: "I am the LORD, that is My name; and My glory I will not give to another!" You and I stood before a craftsman who made us, and He did not wish us to worship another god, quick to anger (Ze'ir Anpin), apart from Him, although he is His agent to perform some action. And why do we not heed His voice to worship Him, and go and worship Ze'ir Anpin, which He did not command us?

Grammar
  • ואת זה חזיתי: the object marker את with the conjunction introduces זה, 'this', ahead of the verb; the English brings it to the front.
  • הלא, האם, וכי and the questions ending in הנעבוד and נעבוד are rhetorical questions that expect the answer 'no'.
  • ונעבוד, נעבוד, נשמע and נלך are first-person plural forms ('we shall worship', 'we shall heed'), read as deliberative in these questions; the English keeps 'we' in each.
  • ישרצו, תוצא and תדשא are jussive in form (Gen 1:20, 1:24, 1:11): 'let the waters swarm', 'let the earth bring forth', 'let the earth sprout'.
  • והיתה תשובתך, לפי ששאר המידות ...: the writer summarises the respondent's reply in indirect speech, with no quotation and no quotation marks.
  • בנו is ב + נו, 'upon us' (not 'in him'); פועלם is 'their Maker' (the participle with a suffix, as הבורא above). In 'וברוב המלאכות נופח ... ומוציא' the participles are singular ('one blows ... brings out'), after Isa 54:16.

The writer, who asked the question (שאלתיך), speaks to the respondent as 'you' and reports the reply in indirect speech; the reply is not quoted. השי"ת is rendered 'the Name, may He be blessed' by the default in the decisions (open question 3).

Other readings (3)
  • כי: that plain 'that' כי can introduce the content of the reply ('I will tell ... that you replied ...') as well as give a reason.
  • ובמעמד הנבחר: at the chosen Standing literal מעמד, 'standing', as in מעמד הר סיני; the English chooses 'assembly'.
  • לז"א אשר לא ציוונו: Ze'ir Anpin, who did not command us Ze'ir Anpin as subject אשר לא ציוונו has no object; it may be God who did not command us (to worship him) or Ze'ir Anpin who gave us no command.
Apparatus
  • Deut 33:14, quoted after 'as it is said'.
  • Gen 1:20, Gen 1:24 and Gen 1:11, quoted with no formula.
  • Ps 104:4, introduced by 'and it is said'.
  • Exod 20:2-3, quoted with no formula; the ellipsis is the fixed rendering of the two verses.
  • Isa 42:8, introduced by 'and it is said'.
  • Exod 34:6, the verse that sets 'slow to anger' against 'quick to anger' (see token 2:12.257).
  • Isa 54:16: 'נפח באש פחם ומוציא כלי למעשהו', echoed in 'נופח באש פחם ומוציא כלי למעשהו'.
  • Joel 2:11: 'ויהוה נתן קולו לפני חילו', echoed in 'נתן קולו לפני חילו'.
  • The Hebrew has a comma between Exod 20:2 and 20:3 and no וגו'; the ellipsis in the English is the fixed rendering (see the question on token 2:12.228).
2:13

As for your questions that you wrote, that one should ask about what the Rambam of blessed memory wrote: "Let him direct his heart toward the Shekhinah and pray," and in Moreh Nevukhim he wrote that the Shekhinah is a created light, etc. Behold, in your question you have revealed that you are wise in your own eyes and have not learned discipline. Is it, then, the way of one who is asked to question his questioner? In any case I will not withhold my quill from replying, even though you have not acted properly! And I say that it is plain and known to every learned man well versed in the books of Israel that the name Shekhinah is said of 3 things: either of the Name, may He be blessed, as our Master wrote in Laws of Repentance, chapter 7: "Great is repentance, which brings a person near to the Shekhinah, as it is said: 'Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God,' etc., and it is said: 'Yet you did not return to Me, says the LORD,' and it is said: 'If you return, O Israel, to Me you shall return.' That is to say, if you turn in repentance, you will cleave to Me, etc." Again there, on the excellence of repentance: "Yesterday this man was separated from the LORD, the God of Israel, etc., and today he is attached to the Shekhinah, as it is said: 'And you who cleave to the LORD your God,' he cries out and is answered at once, as it is said: 'And it shall be that before they call, I will answer.'" And so is the sense of his words in Laws of Prayer, that if he was in a place where he cannot determine the directions, etc. And so our forebears rendered it: "And if he is in a place and cannot tell the direction, let him direct his heart to his Creator and pray."

Grammar
  • Opening: the questioner has raised a contradiction between two statements of the Rambam; the reply first rebukes him (the rhetorical question and the exclamation) and only then answers.
  • The answer is built on a list: the name Shekhinah is said of 3 things, introduced by the particle for the first one (either ... ), and continued in 2:14 (the second) and 2:15 (the third).
  • Quotations inside quotations: the two passages from the Rambam's Laws of Repentance carry five verses between them (Hos 14:2, Amos 4:6, Jer 4:1; Deut 4:4, Isa 65:24), each introduced by the niphal formula 'as it is said' or 'and it is said'; 'that is to say' (kelomar) glosses Jer 4:1 and stands inside the quotation as the author gives it.
  • The participles in the Rambam's sentences ('separated', 'attached', 'cries out and is answered') describe a state, not a past event; 'separated' and 'attached' are passive participles.
  • The last sentence is Judeo-Arabic (Arabic words in Hebrew letters): a one-line proverb, introduced by 'so our forebears rendered it'. It opens with wa-in, 'and if', followed by the verb kana, 'is'.

The reply claims that the Rambam uses the word Shekhinah in three senses, which resolves the apparent contradiction between the Laws of Prayer ('toward the Shekhinah') and the Guide ('a created light'). The Arabic proverb is translated from the Arabic as it stands. The word the text writes with the letters bet, vav, tzadi, ayin is read letter by letter as bawdi' (cf. mawdi', 'place'; buqca, 'spot', is the alternative, with the same sense), and the word written with an abbreviation mark as yuhayyi'; both readings are the translator's, since the pack offers no lexicon for Judeo-Arabic. The proverb is presented as the Arabic rendering of the Rambam's rule in the Laws of Prayer, and the sense of rendered (he'etiku) is given in the token note. The Rambam passages are translated from the Hebrew the author quotes.

Other readings (1)
  • העתיקו: copied alternative sense of he'etiku The verb can mean 'copied over' as well as 'translated'; the English takes 'rendered' (decisions, pilot ruling).
Apparatus
  • Verse: Hos 14:2 ('Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God').
  • Verse: Amos 4:6 ('Yet you did not return to Me, says the LORD').
  • Verse: Jer 4:1; the author's text omits the words 'says the LORD' that stand after 'O Israel' in the verse, and the English follows his wording.
  • Verse: Deut 4:4 ('And you who cleave to the LORD your God', cut off at the comma).
  • Verse: Isa 65:24 ('And it shall be that before they call, I will answer').
  • Allusion: Prov 3:7 ('Do not be wise in your own eyes'); the English of 'wise in your own eyes' is embedded without quotation marks.
  • Judeo-Arabic proverb: wa-in kana fi bawdi' wa-la yuhsin yacrif al-jiha yuhayyi' qalbahu ila khaliqihi wa-yusalli. Two spellings are uncertain: bet-vav-tzadi-ayin, read bawdi' (cf. mawdi', 'place'; alternative buqca, 'spot', the same sense); and the word with the abbreviation mark, read yuhayyi' ('prepares, makes ready'; the English 'direct' follows the context and the Rambam's own 'direct his heart'). Both are translated as the evident word.
2:14

And the second is in a place where the name "the revelation of the Shekhinah" is mentioned, for example, regarding Abraham our father when he went to bind Isaac, of whom it is said: "And he saw the place from afar." Our Rabbis of blessed memory said that he saw a light from afar on Mount Moriah, and as the liturgical poet said: "And he saw a likeness of glory, splendor and honor, and further asked his young men, 'A light: did you see it shining on the top of Mount ha-Mor?' etc." This is the created light that our Master wrote of. And so at the bush: "and he saw, and behold, the bush was burning with fire," and explicitly it is said there: "And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the bush," and this is a created light. And so in every place where the name "the revelation of the Shekhinah" is mentioned, it is a created light.

and-the-second in-a-place that-is-mentioned name revelation-of Shekhinah for-example regarding Abraham our-father when-he-went to-bind [object-marker] Isaac that-is-said of-him and-he-saw [object-marker] the-place from-afar and-said our-Rabbis-of-blessed-memory that-he-saw light from-afar on-mount the-Moriah and-as said the-poet and-he-saw likeness-of glory and-splendor and-honor and-asked further [object-marker] his-young-men light did-you-see shining on-top-of mount the-Mor etc. this-is light created that-wrote our-Master and-so at-the-bush and-he-saw and-behold the-bush burning with-fire and-explicitly it-is-said there and-appeared angel-of the-LORD to-him in-flame-of fire from-within the-bush and-this-is light created and-so every place that-is-mentioned name revelation-of Shekhinah it light created

Grammar
  • The second sense is identified by a phrase that the text itself sets in quotation marks: the revelation of the Shekhinah. The word shem after the verb 'is mentioned' may be 'name' or 'there'; the English takes 'name' (as in 2:13, 'the name Shekhinah') and keeps the quotation marks of the text.
  • Three witnesses for one light: the Rabbis on Mount Moriah, a liturgical poet, and the burning bush. Each is brought by a different formula: 'said', 'as the poet said', and a bare quotation of the verse at the bush.
  • The same verb is used in Hebrew for 'saw' and 'appeared' (vayar / vayera): Abraham 'saw' the place; the angel 'appeared' to Moses in the fire.
  • The poet's question begins with a ha- that makes it interrogative ('did you see'), and his phrase 'Mount ha-Mor' is a form of Moriah.
  • The conclusion is a rule: wherever the revelation of the Shekhinah is mentioned, it is a created light.

The word shem in 'where the name ... is mentioned' may be 'name' or 'there'; the English takes 'name', as in 'the name Shekhinah' in 2:13, and the other reading is in the apparatus and the readings. The text has the participle 'burning' (bo'er, with a vav) in the bush verse, as Exod 3:2 has the participle. The poet is not named and the quoted lines are not identified.

Other readings (2)
  • שם: there shem as the adverb 'in a place where, there, "the revelation of the Shekhinah" is mentioned'; the English takes 'name' (decisions, pilot ruling).
  • שם: there shem as the adverb The same alternative at the close of the rule.
Apparatus
  • Verse: Gen 22:4 ('And he saw the place from afar').
  • Verse: Exod 3:2. 'And he saw, and behold, the bush was burning with fire' is the second half of the verse (the participle bo'er, which the author spells with a vav); 'And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the bush' is the first half, which the author quotes second.
  • The poetic lines are quoted from an unnamed liturgical poem; no source is given and none is added.
  • Alternative reading: shem as 'there' ('in a place where "the revelation of the Shekhinah" is mentioned there'), in 2:14.4 and 2:14.77; the English takes 'name'.
2:15

And the third: the providence of the Name, may He be blessed, over us is also called Shekhinah, as our Rabbis of blessed memory said: "They went into exile to Babylon; the Shekhinah was with them." That is to say, His providence, may He be blessed, clung to us, as He promised us in the Torah: "And yet even so, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them and I will not abhor them so as to destroy them, to break My covenant with them, for I am the LORD their God." And so it is with everything of the kind. Every place is to be understood according to its subject in one of these three mentioned aspects.

and-the-third the-providence-of the-Name-may-He-be-blessed over-us is-called also Shekhinah as said our-Rabbis-of-blessed-memory they-went-into-exile to-Babylon Shekhinah with-them that-is-to-say his-providence may-He-be-blessed clung to-us as He-promised-us in-the-Torah and-even also this when-they-are in-land-of their-enemies not I-rejected-them and-not I-abhorred-them to-destroy-them to-break my-covenant with-them for I the-LORD their-God and-so every like-this every place is-understood according-to its-subject in-one from-three aspects these the-mentioned

Grammar
  • The third sense is God's providence over His people. The proof is a rabbinic saying with no verb for the second clause (the Shekhinah with them) and a verse from the Torah.
  • The verb of the promise in the verse is a perfect, 'I have not rejected them', which in this context states a promise about the future, as the English renders it.
  • Dabekah in 'clung to us' is feminine to agree with 'providence'; the verb 'clung' reuses the stem of the word the Rambam used for repentance (2:13).
  • The paragraph closes with a rule: each occurrence of the word is to be understood according to its subject as one of the three senses.

The rabbinic saying is quoted without a source; none is added. The verse is Lev 26:44 as the author gives it. His spelling of two words differs from the verse; the meaning is not affected.

Other readings (1)
  • לא מאסתים ולא געלתים: I have not rejected them and I have not abhorred them perfect as written The verbs are perfects (Lev 26:44); the English takes them as a promise about the future, which the author's 'as He promised us' supports.
Apparatus
  • Verse: Lev 26:44 ('And yet even so, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them ... for I am the LORD their God'); the author's text spells 'their enemies' and 'to destroy them' with an added vav.
  • Rabbinic saying: 'They went into exile to Babylon; the Shekhinah was with them'; no source is given.
2:16

And as for what you wrote: "And more than this, what he wrote about the glory of the LORD that it is created light, if so, how were Israel going out at the entrance of their tents and bowing down to the created thing?" Not to the visible glory do they bow down, but only to Him who made His glory dwell there. And the visible glory is there as a sign and a token for them, for the Name, may He be blessed, desired the tent of meeting as His dwelling, just as we bow down and pray to the Name, may He be blessed, toward the Temple and Jerusalem, for the LORD chose Zion; He desired it as His dwelling. And the Rambam had already explained in chapter 64 of the first, that the glory of the LORD sometimes denotes the created light, which the Holy One makes dwell in the place, as "and the glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and covered it, etc." and sometimes by it they mean His essence, may He be blessed, and His reality, as in "show me, please, Your glory," and the answer came: "for no man shall see Me and live," which shows that the glory spoken of here is His very essence, may He be blessed, and he said "Your glory," to magnify, etc. And similarly we find in the words of our Rabbis of blessed memory that the name Elohim is equivocal, applying to judges and to angels, and to the Name, may He be blessed. Also, the name Shekhinah is equivocal, applying to what I mentioned above. And I saw fit to alert you here that there is no prohibition on bowing down to a man, so long as his intent is not to accept him as God, and he is not worshipped, but only submits to him and humbles himself before him, or by way of acknowledgment for a kindness that he did for him. For indeed Abraham our father bowed down to the sons of Heth for the kindness they did with him, to give him a burial place. And so Rabbi Saadia Gaon rendered: "and bowed down to the people of the land, to the sons of Heth, and prostrated to the people of the land that He created." And Joshua bowed down to the angel. And Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba bowed down to David. And we find much in the verses that they bowed down to the created being. And we read in Sanhedrin, chapter Four Deaths (Sanhedrin 61b): It was stated: "One who worships idolatry out of love and out of fear, Abaye says: he is liable, for he worshipped it. Rava says: he is exempt. If he accepted it upon himself as God, yes; if not, no. And Abaye said: How do I know this? for we learned: 'One who worships idolatry: one who worships, and one who sacrifices, and one who burns incense, and one who pours libations, and one who bows down, and one who accepts it upon himself as God, and one who says to him: You are my God.' What? Is it not that 'one who worships' means out of love or out of fear? And Rava says to you: No, but as Rabbi Yirmiyah resolves it: (Rashi explains: one who worships every worship that is customary for it, and one who sacrifices, etc., not in its customary way, and in every case the first clause and the last are for the sake of divinity). Abaye said: How do I know this? for it was taught: 'You shall not bow down to them; to them you do not bow down, but you bow down to a man like yourself.' One might think: even to worship like Haman? Scripture says: 'and you shall not worship them.' But Haman was worshipped out of fear! And Rava? Like Haman, and not like Haman. Like Haman, for he himself is idolatry; and not like Haman, for in the case of Haman it was out of fear, and here it is not out of fear. And Abaye said: How do I know this? for it was taught: 'An anointed priest in idolatry. Rabbi says: in an unwitting act, and the Sages say: in a concealed matter, and they agree that for a she-goat it is like an individual, and they agree that he does not bring a suspended guilt offering.' What is this unwitting act like? If he holds that it is a synagogue and bowed down to it, then his heart is with Heaven. But suppose he saw a statue and bowed down to it, (explanation: that he saw the figure of the king, which they were accustomed to make in the likeness of the king, and one who saw it bows down to it in honor of the king, and sometimes they worship it, and this one saw one who was worshipped and bowed down to it). If he accepted it upon himself as God, it is deliberate; and if he did not accept it upon himself as God, it is nothing. (Rashi explains: but he bowed down to him in honor of the king; it is nothing, for he did not intend idolatry). But is it not out of love and out of fear? And Rava says to you: In the case of one who says 'permitted.' Does 'says permitted' mean concealment of a matter? In the case of one who says permitted entirely; concealment of a matter is upholding part and nullifying part." Thus far the Gemara, with some of Rashi's explanation. And a matter is learned: that to every created being it is forbidden to bow down, except a man, provided that he not be worshipped like Haman, who made himself idolatry, (as we said in Megillah 19), for otherwise Mordecai would not have refrained from bowing down to him, as it is taught in the baraita: "You shall not bow down to them; to them you do not bow down, but you bow down to a man like yourself," provided that he not be worshipped like Haman, who made himself God, but one only bows down to him as a sign of honor, and not for divinity, and therefore Joshua bowed down to the angel, since he appeared to him in the form of a man, as it is written: "And behold, a man was standing opposite him," and therefore he bowed down to him as a sign of honor and not to worship him. And see in Sefer ha-Ikkarim, Treatise 2, chapter 28, where he elaborated on the verses that call the glory that appears to the prophets by the name YHVH, and also the ark, as it says: "And it was when the ark set out, etc. Arise, LORD, and when it rested he said: Return, LORD." And Joshua called the ark "Lord of all the earth"; see there. And in his view, that Joshua bowed down to the angel, because that bowing was in honor of the Name, may He be blessed, and since this one was His messenger, etc.; see there. And our Rabbis of blessed memory said: "Bow down to the fox in its time," that is to say: a man lowly and despised like a fox, and the moment stands for him in some office that is in his hand: bow down to him. And so it is customary with us and with the Arabs to bow down and kiss a man of high rank, and there is no prohibition in this, for he does not accept him as God; it is only as a sign of honor that he bows down to him and kisses his feet.

Grammar
  • The paragraph is the respondent's reply in the correspondence of chapter 2. 'What you wrote' answers the questioner, and the question from 'And as for what you wrote' to 'created thing?' is his.
  • The main sense turns on the Bavli passage (Sanhedrin 61b), Bavli Aramaic, quoted from 'It was stated' to 'Thus far the Gemara'. Its Aramaic forms are glossed in the tokens (פלחה, קבליה, דהא, אי ... אין). The author's two Rashi glosses and his explanation of the statue are in parentheses inside it.
  • The Hebrew for 'not to the visible glory do they bow down' puts the negated object first. The English keeps that order, and 'but only' (רק) then answers it.
  • שהשרה is causative (made dwell): 'to him who made His glory dwell there'. The verse cited, Exod 24:16, is cut short by the author's 'וכו'', and the English keeps the 'etc.'.
  • Two verbs carry the argument: נעבד (passive, 'is worshipped') and נכנע ('submits'). The author separates bowing as worship from bowing as submission or thanks, so the English keeps the two apart.
  • Saadia's rendering of Gen 23:7 is Judeo-Arabic in Hebrew letters: וסגד לאהל אלבלד is Arabic 'and he prostrated to the people of the land' (אהל is ahl, 'people of'); the word שברא after it is unexplained.
  • משותף is the Maimonidean term for an equivocal word; the author says the names אלהים and שכינה each name several things, which is why a created thing may be called 'glory' and the bowing in Exod 33 is to the One who caused it to dwell.

The reply quotes the questioner and the Gemara, and its Saadia and Joshua examples are kept as the author gives them.

Other readings (1)
  • לעבד כהמן: a slave like Haman plain reading of לעבד as a noun The unpointed לעבד may be 'to a slave'; the answer, 'and you shall not worship them', favours 'to worship' or 'to one worshipped'.
Ancient Near East
  • The anderta (אנדרטא) in the Gemara quotation is an image or statue; the author's Rashi gloss reads it as 'a figure of the king'.
  • The anointed priest (כהן משיח) of the Gemara quotation is the priest anointed for office (Lev 4:3).
  • Gen 23 tells of Abraham's purchase of a burial place from the sons of Heth (Gen 23:3-20).
Apparatus

  • Ps 132:13 (embedded, no marks): 'כי בחר ה' בציון אוה למושב לו'.

2:17

And greater than this is what they also do: they sacrifice sheep and cattle before a king or a minister. It is one of the inner worships. Whoever does it for one of the kinds of idolatry, even though its worship is not in that way, is liable, as we learned in Sanhedrin, in the chapter “Four Death Penalties”: “The worshipper of idolatry: one who worships, and one who sacrifices, and one who burns incense, and one who pours libation, and one who bows down, etc.” And we say in the Gemara: On this: “What is ‘one who worships’?” Rabbi Yirmiyah said: “This is what it means: one who worships in the usual way, and one who sacrifices, and one who burns incense, and one who pours libation, and one who bows down, even not in the usual way.” And so all the decisors ruled that for the four worships one is liable even if not in the usual way. And this practice is still observed to this day among our brethren, the people of the villages and the towns: that if one of them had an enemy who seeks his harm, he brings a lamb and slaughters it before his minister, to save him from his enemy. And Scripture also says: “Offer it now to your governor, etc.” Our forebears also had this rule: when the king came to the province, they would sacrifice an ox before him, and they would take the price of the ox from the communal chest. And they heard of no one who doubted this on account of idolatry, since one does not intend to worship him by this or to accept him upon oneself as a god; it is only a sign of honor that one makes to him. Our father Jacob, peace be upon him, said to his sons: “Take of the choicest of the land's produce in your vessels, and bring down to the man a gift,” and it is said: “And they brought him the gift that was in their hands to the house, and bowed down to him, faces, etc.” And concerning Saul, the LORD's chosen one, it is said: “And sons of Belial said, ‘How can this one save us?’ and did not bring him a gift.” And in Nedarim we learned: “One who vowed by an offering and said, ‘I vowed only by the offerings of kings.’” So it is clear that bowing down, sacrifice, presenting a gift, and all four inner worships are permitted to do for a man who is not worshipped like Haman; but if he is worshipped like Haman it is forbidden, for Mordechai refrained from bowing down to Haman, because he made himself an object of idolatry.

Grammar
  • שעושים לזבוח: the relative clause שעושים ('that they do') governs the infinitive לזבוח ('to sacrifice'); the object is 'sheep and cattle' and the place is 'before a king or a minister'. והיא refers back to that act, and עבודות פנים is the Mishnah's term for the inner worships.
  • Bavli Aramaic: ואמרינן ('and we say'), עלה ('on it', the Mishnah), מאי ('what is'), הכי קאמר ('this is what he means'); the Gemara asks what the Mishnah's first 'one who worships' means, and Rabbi Yirmiyah answers.
  • Mishnaic Hebrew: the Mishnah's list has four participles with ה: העובד, המזבח ('one who sacrifices'), המקטר ('one who burns incense'), המנסך ('one who pours libation'), and המשתחוה. The Mishnah quotation is cut off by וכו'; the words ואפי' שלא כדרכה ('even not in the usual way') belong to Rabbi Yirmiyah's explanation, and the author repeats them in his own ruling.
  • בסנהדרין פ' ד' מיתות: ד' stands for ארבע, so the words are the title of the chapter, 'Four Death Penalties'; the English does not turn it into 'chapter four'.
  • נעבד (passive, 'is worshipped'), נמנע ('refrained') and the adjective אסור ('forbidden') carry the last sentences; the English keeps the passive, and the participle ונוטלים ('and they take') is habitual.
  • שאם היה לאחד מהם אויב ... הוא מביא: a past verb in the conditional clause and a present verb in the main clause, with a habitual sense: 'if one of them had an enemy, he brings'.

The Mishnah's list and Rabbi Yirmiyah's gloss are given as the author quotes them; המזבח is 'one who sacrifices'. 'Idolatry' and 'inner worships' follow the fixed terms. פ' ד' מיתות is read as the chapter's title, 'Four Death Penalties' (ד' = ארבע), not as 'chapter four'.

Other readings (3)
  • פ ד מיתות: chapter four, death penalties plain numeral The letters could be read as the numeral 4 followed by מיתות; the English reads ד' as ארבע, the chapter's title.
  • לעבדו: to serve him plain sense of עבד עבד also means serve a master; here, with ולקבלו עליו באלוה, it is the worship due to a god.
  • באלוה: as God ruling on אלוה The ruling on singular אלוה would give 'God'; kept as 'a god' because the king is the object.
Apparatus
  • Mal 1:8: 'הקריבהו נא לפחתך' (Offer it now to your governor), quoted by the author with וכו'.
  • Gen 43:11: 'קחו מזמרת הארץ בכליכם והורידו לאיש מנחה' (Take of the choicest of the land's produce in your vessels and bring down to the man a gift).
  • Gen 43:26: 'ויביאו לו את המנחה אשר בידם הביתה'; the verse continues 'וישתחוו לו ארצה'. The author's 'וישתחו לו אפים וכו'' has the wording of Gen 42:6 ('וישתחוו לו אפים ארצה'); the English follows his wording.
  • 1 Sam 10:27: 'ובני בליעל אמרו מה יושיענו זה ולא הביאו לו מנחה'; the verse has an extra clause, 'ויבזהו', before 'ולא הביאו' that the author omits, and the English omits it too.
  • 'בחיר ה'' for Saul echoes 2 Sam 21:6 ('Saul, the chosen of the LORD').
  • Esth 3:2: Mordechai's refusal to bow to Haman, given by the author in his own words.
  • The Mishnah of Sanhedrin is cited as 'פ' ד' מיתות', read as the chapter's title 'Four Death Penalties'; the reference is kept as written and none is added.
  • The quotation from Nedarim gives no reference, and none is added.
2:18

And in the book Teshu'at Yisrael by Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel he wrote, and these are his words: “I have been required to make known the customs of honor and submission with which the Jews honor the Torah scroll, for our enemies, who do not know what this is, provoke us, saying that we are worshippers of idols, and that we bow down to a wooden ark and to the sheets of skin within it. Therefore I shall set out my reply in proper order, as the good hand of the LORD is upon me, namely, every man of Israel will see himself obliged to rise and stand at the removal of a Torah scroll from the holy ark until it is placed on the reading platform, to show it to all the people and to read from it. And we find that they did so in the days of Nehemiah, as it is written: ‘And when he opened, all the people stood.’ And this they do out of the fear and honor with which they honor the words of the living God written in it, and for that same reason they bow their heads when carrying it from the ark to the reading platform, and not because of any other of the reasons that we shall mention.”

Grammar
  • נדרשתי להודיע: a niphal perfect, 'I have been required', with the infinitive להודיע, 'to make known'; the first person is the letter-writer's, quoted by the author.
  • ככתוב וכפתחו עמדו כל העם: וכפתחו is a temporal clause ('when he opened'); עמדו is third plural, 'they stood'; the quotation is inside the quoted letter, so it takes single marks.
  • והוא כל איש ישראל יראה: והוא introduces the content ('namely'); יראה is a yiqtol with a future sense, 'will see himself obliged'.
  • ולא משום דבר אחר מן הטעמים אשר נזכיר: the last clause denies every other reason, so the reasons given are the only ones; the witness has no closing formula, and the quotation runs to the end of the paragraph.

The letter is the one Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel is quoted as writing; 'the reading platform' renders tevah. The witness has no closing formula, so the quotation runs to the end of the paragraph.

Apparatus
  • Allusion to Neh 2:8 ('כיד אלהי הטובה עלי'; cf. Ezra 7:9, 8:18, 7:28); the English follows the author's wording.
  • Allusion to Jer 23:36 ('דברי אלהים חיים'; cf. Jer 10:10, Deut 5:23 for 'אלהים חיים').
  • Neh 8:5: the author writes 'וכפתחו עמדו כל העם'; his wording is followed.
  • The title of the book is transliterated per the project scheme; its meaning is at token 2.
2:19

The first: there is a great difference between one who worships and prays to something, and one who only honours something. To pray to something and to worship something with worship is forbidden to us, whether it be a man or an angel, corporeal or spiritual; but to bestow honour, as a youth honours an elder, a servant his master, and the lowly the honoured, is permitted. So too we find of our father Abraham, who believed in the LORD, that he shattered the monuments of idols and disowned them, and bowed down to the ground before three angels standing over him, even though they appeared to him as men. So too Joshua did at Jericho: when he saw a man standing before him and took him for an angel, he fell to the ground before him. And if men of understanding like them, in whose ways we walk and from the commandments of whose lips we do not shrink, did this, and it was not counted to them as a sin of idolatry; it is clear that to honour a Torah scroll is not the worship of idols.
