Grammar
  • בין ... ובין frames the contrast: the second half is elliptical, so 'one who only honours' is set against 'one who worships and prays'.
  • ולעבוד עבודה: the verb and its noun share a root; the English keeps 'worship' for both, as the Hebrew does.
  • כמו שיכבד הנער את הזקן: the comparison gives the model of honour the author permits; the paragraph's argument turns on the difference between the two.
  • ואם אנשי לבב ... עשו זאת ... ברור הוא כי: the 'if' clause gives the case of the patriarchs and Joshua; the main clause is 'it is clear that'.
Apparatus
  • Text translated from Wikisource as the base text; not yet collated with the 1931 scan.
  • Gen 15:6: 'אשר האמין בה'' echoes 'והאמן בה''.
  • Gen 18:2: the verse behind 'השתחווה ארצה לפני שלשה מלאכים' (Abraham bows to the ground before the three men); the author calls them angels.
  • Josh 5:13-14: the verse behind Joshua's falling to the ground before the man who stands before him.
  • Job 34:10: אנשי לבב, 'men of understanding'.
  • Job 23:12: cf. 'מצות שפתיו ולא אמיש'; the printed נבוש may be a variant of נמוש (see the note on 2:19.90).
2:20

Second: the Jews are very careful in matters of other worship, and even to appear as one who honours it is forbidden to them. As they said in the Talmud and in the Rambam: "If a man turned aside from the road he was taking near a house of idolatry, and a thorn lodged in his foot, he may not bend, nor even kneel and bow down to remove it there, so that he should not appear in the eyes of passers-by as one who bows down and honours idolatry." And if the prostration before the Ark were like other worship, the Jews would not have kept this custom; and since they kept it from the days of their fathers, it is a sign of truth that it is not corrupted.

Grammar
  • כמו שאמרו בתלמוד וברמב"ם: the formula אמרו introduces the passage that follows, which is therefore in quotation marks; no reference is given.
  • לא ישח אף לא יכרע וישתחוה להוציאו: the negative governs all three verbs: he may not stoop, nor even kneel and bow down; the clause 'so that he should not appear' gives the reason.
  • ואם היתה ... לא היו היהודים מחזיקים: a counterfactual, both clauses in the past; the author argues from what the Jews would not have done.
  • וכיון שהחזיקו בו מימי אבותיהם אות אמת הוא כי אינה משובשת: the argument from custom; 'since they kept it' is causal, and 'that it is not corrupted' gives the sign's content.
Ancient Near East
  • The Ark (הארון): the cabinet in the synagogue in which the Torah scrolls are kept; the custom the author describes is bowing before it.
Apparatus
  • Job 6:18: cf. 'ילפתו ארחות דרכם' (they turn aside the paths of their way), the source of the wording לפת ארחות דרכו.
  • The author names no tractate or chapter for the Talmud and Rambam passage.
2:21

Third: one of the customs of honour by which they once honoured idolatry was kissing. So too we find in Scripture: "And I will leave in Israel seven thousand, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him." And it is said: "Those who sacrifice men kiss calves." And if it is so, will all who kiss the Torah scroll be worshippers of idols? But the matter is not so, for this is only honour, that they honour their Torah, and not worship; and therefore the prostration before the Ark is also only honour and not worship.

Grammar
  • וכן מצינו במקרא: the verse is 1 Kgs 19:18, quoted in the words of the verse; 'we find' introduces it without a formula.
  • ונאמר זובחי אדם עגלים ישקון: the second verse, Hos 13:2, with the spelling זובחי (the verse has זבחי); the subject is the sacrificers and ישקון is the plural imperfect, 'kiss' (or, as a wish, 'let them kiss').
  • ואם כן הוא יהיו כל המנשקים ... עובדי ע"ז?: a question about the future, answered by 'but this is not so'.
  • כי אין זה רק כבוד שיכבדו את תורתם ולא עבודה: 'for this is only honour, that they honour their Torah and not worship' explains 'this'.
Ancient Near East
  • Baal: the god of the Canaanites, whose worship Elijah opposed (1 Kgs 18); the verse the author quotes is set in that story.
Apparatus
  • 1 Kgs 19:18: quoted in the verse's own words.
  • Hos 13:2: the author writes זובחי, the verse זבחי; ישקון may also be read as a wish, 'let them kiss calves'.
2:22

Fourth: experience has taught us that in all the languages of the nations customs of honour are found, by which a man honours his fellow when they meet, and so they bow their heads, one opposite the other, and this too has been for us a sign that it is not the worship of idols, but customs of honour.

fourth experience taught us that in-all languages-of the-nations were-found customs-of the-honour; they-honour by-them a-man [object] his-fellow when-they-meet; and-so they-bow their-heads one opposite the-other; and-it-was this too for-us for-a-sign that-it-is-not the-worship-of idols; but customs-of honour.

Grammar
  • הנסיון הורה אותנו: the subject is 'experience' and the verb is hiphil, 'taught us'.
  • יכבדו בם איש את רעהו בהיפגשם: 'by them' refers back to the customs; ב plus the infinitive with a suffix gives 'when they meet'.
  • וכן יכופו ראשיהם זה לעומת זה: 'one opposite the other' is the reciprocal phrase of the bowing.
  • והיה גם זה לנו לאות שאינה עבודת גלולים: the sign (אות) is the clause that follows: 'that it is not the worship of idols'.
Apparatus
  • Eccl 7:14: cf. 'זה לעמת זה' (the one over against the other).
2:23

"Fifth: the people who dwell in Asia, if a written command from the king comes to them, they take it in their hands, kiss it with their mouths and place it on their heads. How much more so shall we honor the words of the living God, King over all the earth.

fifth the-people the-dwelling in-Asia if comes to-them written-command from-the-king in-their-hands they-seize-it, with-their-mouths they-kiss-it, and-on their-heads they-place-it, how-much-more so we-shall-honor the-words-of God living King over all the-earth

Grammar
  • The paragraph is the fifth point of a numbered series, and its number opens the English as it opens the Hebrew.
  • The conditional אם takes yiqtol verbs (they take, kiss, place): these describe a habitual practice, so the English uses the present.
  • The argument is from the lesser to the greater (qal wa-chomer): if the people honor a king's written command, 'how much more so' the words of God. נכבד, with the pronoun אנו before it, is the plain imperfect, 'we shall honor'.
  • The three acts (seizing in the hands, kissing with the mouth, placing on the head) are parallel clauses, and the English keeps their order.

Quotation: Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, Teshu'at Yisrael, begins at 2:18 ('and these are his words') and continues through 2:25, where 'Thus far his words' closes it. Proposed ruling: each paragraph of a quotation that runs across paragraphs opens with a double quotation mark, and only the last closes (so 2:19-2:22 and 2:24 open with one; 2:18 does not close). In this unit 2:23, 2:24 and 2:25 follow it.

Apparatus
  • Base text from Wikisource; the 1931 scan is not yet collated, so the paragraph is translated as the base text (decisions, Q2).
  • Quotation: this paragraph is part of a quotation from the book Teshu'at Yisrael of Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, introduced at 2:18 with 'and these are his words'. It runs through 2:25, where עכ"ל closes it. The opening mark here is the paragraph-opening mark of a quotation that continues across paragraphs; the quotation does not begin at 2:23.
  • Allusions, the author's wording and not a quotation: 'the words of the living God' (Jer 23:36, דברי אלהים חיים; cf. Jer 10:10) and 'King over all the earth' (cf. Zech 14:9; Ps 47:3).
2:24

"Sixth: when the seventy-two elders brought the Torah to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, he rose from his throne and bowed down seven times to meet it, and if a worshipper of idols, who has not put his neck under the yoke of our Torah, honored it so much, how much more so we who enter into its covenant and to whom it was given as an inheritance.

sixth when-they-brought seventy and-two elders (object) the-Torah to-Ptolemy king of-Egypt rose from-his-throne and-bowed-down seven times to-meet-it, and-if worshipper-of idols who not put his-neck into-the-yoke of-our-Torah honored-it so much, how-much-more so we entering in-its-covenant and-to-whom it-was-given to-us as-inheritance

Grammar
  • The temporal clause כשהביאו puts the verb first and the subject after it: 'when the seventy-two elders brought the Torah'.
  • קם ... והשתחוה are two past acts in sequence (qatal with vav); the English keeps the sequence, 'rose ... and bowed down'.
  • The ואם clause is complete: 'and if a worshipper of idols, who has not put his neck under the yoke of our Torah, honored it so much' (כבדה, piel perfect with the suffix 'it'); the apodosis is 'how much more so we ...'.
  • הביא צוארו בעול is an idiom for accepting a burden: 'brought his neck under the yoke'. In ואשר ניתנה לנו למורשה the verb ניתנה is feminine, so the Torah is what was given, 'as an inheritance' (Deut 33:4); the English reads 'to whom it was given'.
Ancient Near East
  • The Greek translation of the Torah, made in Alexandria in the third century BCE, is attributed in the rabbinic tradition to seventy-two elders in the time of Ptolemy, king of Egypt. The author follows that tradition.
Apparatus
  • Allusion, not quoted: Deut 33:4 for 'למורשה' ('an inheritance').
  • The number seventy-two and the translation story are the author's (see context).
2:25

"Seventh: the foundations and principles of our religion are the existence of one, unique, eternal Creator, who is not a body, nor a force in a body, who gives the Torah to His people Israel through the faithful lawgiver Moses, servant of the LORD, master of all the prophets. He, may He be blessed, looks on and exercises providence over the worlds that He created. And His eyes roam over all, and He searches and examines the hearts of the sons of man and judges justly concerning the deeds of a man's steps. From Him alone we seek help in our distress, and He will bring forth a shoot from the stock of Jesse, who will gather the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth, and from all the cut-off corners to which they scattered them there, the dry bones of their dead will live, and their corpses will rise. Indeed, all these are the principles and roots of our religion. And what trace of idolatry is found in them? Even in the opinion of those whose opinions and beliefs differ from our opinions and from our faith." Thus far his words.

seventh foundations-of and-principles-of our-religion are existence of-Creator one unique eternal who is-not body nor force in-body giving the-Torah to-his-people Israel through the-hand-of the-lawgiver the-faithful Moses servant of-LORD master of-all the-prophets he may-he-be-blessed who-looks-on and-exercises-providence over the-worlds he-created and-his-eyes roam over-all and-searches and-examines the-hearts of-sons of-man and-judges justly concerning the-deeds-of the-steps-of a-man from-him alone we-seek help in-distress our and-he will-bear-fruit a-shoot from-stock-of Jesse who will-gather outcasts-of Israel from-four corners-of the-earth and-from all the-cut-off corners to-which they-scattered them there the-bones of-their-dead dry will-live and-their-corpses will-rise indeed all these the-principles and-roots-of our-religion and-what trace idolatry is-found in-them even in-the-opinion-of those whose opinions and-beliefs differ from-our-opinions and-from-our-faith thus far his-words

Grammar
  • The paragraph is one sentence: 'the foundations and principles ... are the existence of ...' (הם is plural). Its relative clauses (אשר, נותן) continue from the Creator, and the English keeps the sentence long.
  • The verbs of providence (המציץ, ומשגיח, חוקר, ובוחן, ושופט) are participles with no finite verb; the English makes them finite with 'He'.
  • והוא יפרה נצר: Isa 11:1 has this verb intransitively ('shall bear fruit'); here it takes נצר as its object, and the English follows the author ('bring forth a shoot').
  • The last sentence is a fragment that continues the question: אף לדעת אותם אשר דעותיהם ואמונותיהם נבדלו ..., 'even in the opinion of those whose opinions and beliefs differ ...'. לדעת is 'in the opinion of', not an infinitive. In ועל עלילות מצעדי גבר, עלילות is in the construct: 'concerning the deeds of a man's steps'.
Ancient Near East
  • קצוצי פאה (Jer 9:25): in that verse the phrase names the desert peoples who clip the corners of their hair, a practice that Lev 19:27 forbids to Israel. Here the author uses it of the places (שמה, 'there') to which Israel was scattered; the English keeps the words literally, 'cut-off corners'.
Apparatus
  • Quotation: the double quotation marks close here with the formula עכ"ל. The quotation (Rabbi Menasseh ben Israel, Teshu'at Yisrael) opens at 2:18 (see 2:23 apparatus); the opening mark here is the paragraph-opening mark.
  • Allusions, the author's wording and not quotations: Jer 17:10 (חוקר לב בוחן) for 'searches and examines the hearts'; 2 Chr 16:9 and Zech 4:10 for 'His eyes roam over all'; Prov 20:24 and Ps 37:23 (מצעדי גבר) for 'a man's steps'; Deut 34:5 (משה עבד ה') for 'servant of the LORD'; Isa 11:1 for 'a shoot from the stock of Jesse'; Isa 11:12 (מארבע כנפות הארץ) for 'from the four corners of the earth'; Isa 56:8 and Ps 147:2 (נדחי ישראל) for 'the outcasts of Israel'; Ezek 37 (the dry bones) and Isa 26:19 (נבלתי יקומון) for the resurrection clause; Jer 9:25 for 'cut-off corners'.
2:26

And according to our way, the way of our Rabbis of blessed memory in the aforementioned baraita, there is no need for all this, since our intention is not that we bow down before the Torah scroll, but to Him who chose the Torah. Explicitly, we say: "Come, let us bow down and bend the knee, let us kneel before the LORD our Maker." And as for the bowing down of Abraham our father to the angels, and so Joshua's, if you wish, say: since they appeared to them as men, we apply to them what the Rabbis said in the baraita: "'You shall not bow down to them.' To them you may not bow down, but you bow down to a man like yourself," since they were revealed to them in the form of men. And if you wish, say that the intention of Abraham and Joshua was to bow down to Him who sent them, and as the author of the Ikkarim wrote.

according-to our-way the-way-of our-Rabbis-of-blessed-memory in-the-baraita the-aforementioned there-is-no need for-all this since our-intention is-not that-we bow-down before the-Torah-scroll but to-whom chose the-Torah explicitly we say come let-us-bow-down and-bend-the-knee let-us-kneel before the-LORD our-maker and-the-bowing-down of-Abraham our-father to-the-angels and-so Joshua if-you-wish say since they-appeared to-them as-men we-apply to-them what they-said the-Rabbis in-the-baraita you-shall-not bow-down to-them to-them you-may-not you bow-down but you bow-down to-a-man like-yourself since they-were-revealed to-them in-the-form of-men and-if-you-wish say that-the-intention of-Abraham and-Joshua to-bow-down to-whom they-sent-them and-as the-author-of the-Ikkarim wrote

Grammar
  • בואו נשתחוה ונכרעה נברכה is Ps 95:6, given as the people's words: the cohortatives ('let us') stay in the English, and the verse is set in quotation marks. נכרעה is 'let us bend the knee' and נברכה 'let us kneel' (ברך, not 'bless').
  • והשתחוית is a noun ('the bowing down'), so 'And as for the bowing down' is a topic phrase; the Hebrew joins it by a comma to איבעית אימא, and the English keeps one sentence: 'And as for ... Joshua's, if you wish, say: ...'.
  • איבעית אימא ('if you wish, say') introduces a second explanation. The author gives two, the first (the angels appeared as men) and the second (the intention was toward the One who sent them); the English keeps both in order.
  • The baraita is quoted inside the sentence ('what the Rabbis said in the baraita: ...'), and the English returns to the author's syntax with 'since they were revealed to them'.
  • אי אתה משתחוה is the Talmudic negative of permission, 'you may not bow down'; the English keeps the modal.
Apparatus
  • Ps 95:6 for 'בואו נשתחוה ונכרעה נברכה לפני ה׳ עושנו'.
  • Exod 20:5 for 'לא תשתחוה להם' ('you shall not bow down to them'), the words of the baraita.
  • Cf. Gen 18:2 and Josh 5:14 for the bowing of Abraham and Joshua; the author alludes to them and does not quote them.
2:27

And your question concerning prophecy, although it does not belong to our subject, and you asked only to mislead us and to divert us to another matter, behold, this is set out in the degrees of prophecy in the Rambam, Laws of the Foundations of the Torah, and in part two of the book Moreh Nevukhim, and in the book Emunot ve-De'ot of Rabbi Saadia Gaon. Since I have found you wise in your own eyes, I return to ask you to answer me a decisive answer from the words of our Rabbis of blessed memory in the Talmud, for you alone (in your opinion) all mysteries have been revealed to you, and extraordinary understanding and a new spirit have been given within you. Instruct us, I and my companions, how the matters can agree fully and well. For our soul has longed to hear your teachings, and to delight in your perfect Torah, and it will be to you a merit, and also great honor you will inherit from us.

and-your-question concerning prophecy although is-not relevant to-our-subject and-not you-asked only to-mislead-us and-to-divert-us to-a-matter other. behold this is-set-out the-degrees-of prophecy in-the-Rambam Laws-of the-Foundations-of the-Torah, and-in part two of-the-book the-Moreh, and-in-the-book the-Emunot and-the-De'ot of-Rabbi-Saadia-Gaon. and-since I-found-you wise in-your-eyes, I-return to-ask of-you to-answer to-me an-answer decisive from-the-words-of our-Rabbis in-the-Talmud, for you alone (in-your-opinion) to-you were-revealed all mysteries, and-understanding extraordinary and-spirit new has-been-given within-you. instruct-us I and-my-companions how the-matters will-agree in-one-reed in-full and-good. for our-soul longed to-hear your-teachings, and-to-delight in-your-Torah the-perfect, and-to-you will-be righteousness, and-also honor great you-will-inherit from-us

Grammar
  • The paragraph is a letter, and the list of works (the Rambam, the Moreh, Emunot ve-De'ot) is a series of 'in' phrases; the English keeps the series in the Hebrew's order. The opening ושאלתך ... אעפ"י ... ולא שאלת ... runs on, by commas, to the main clause הנה זה מבואר, and the English keeps it as one sentence.
  • ולא שאלת רק להטעותנו: 'you asked only (nothing but) to mislead us'; לא ... רק is 'not ... except'.
  • חכם בעיניך echoes Prov 3:7 (אל תהי חכם בעיניך), 'wise in your own eyes'; the English follows the verse's sense.
  • הורינו אני וחבירי איך הדברים יעלו: the imperative is followed by a 'how' clause, so the English reads 'Instruct us ..., how the matters can agree'.
Apparatus
  • Cf. Ezek 36:26 for 'ורוח חדש ניתן בקרבך' ('a new spirit ... within you'); the author does not quote it.
  • Prov 3:7 (אל תהי חכם בעיניך) for 'חכם בעיניך' ('wise in your own eyes'); the author alludes to it.
  • Dan 5:12 and 5:14 (רוח יתירה) for 'בינה יתירה' ('extraordinary understanding').
  • Ps 19:8 (תורת ה' תמימה) for 'תורתך התמימה' ('your perfect Torah'); cf. Ps 119:77, 92 (תורתך שעשעי) for 'to delight in your Torah'.
  • Deut 24:13 (ולך תהיה צדקה) for 'ולך תהיה צדקה' ('it will be to you a merit').
  • Prov 3:35 (כבוד חכמים ינחלו) for 'כבוד גדול תנחל' ('great honor you will inherit').
2:28

Reply. To man the arrangements of the heart, and from the LORD the answer of the tongue. And it was when I saw your letter, I sat astonished and dismayed. How your heart emboldened you to inquire and investigate after the band of the Geonim, who are faithful in the Torah, distinguished in lineage, like the seed of the mighty, and after several decisors and also expounders, the early and the later, the sages of the Maghreb, Ashkenaz, Sefarad and the Yemenites. And the rest of the congregations, the holy seed, the faithful children, this is their treasure, more than fine gold and many pearls. Can a stumbling come from the hand of righteous and faithful ones, who know knowledge, the wise and discerning, who fear God and turn aside from evil with their might. By their wisdom they felled many foes and multitudes who stood against them in every age. Can it be that their Kabbalah is compounded in vanity and errors, they who, because of their great wisdom, were approved by the mouths of princes and nobles and stood before kings and rulers, and can fathers and sons walk on a path that is not good? How many hundreds of years is this? And how many of them are distinguished in every wisdom, and scholars, Kabbalists with philosophy and logic, medicine, mathematics and astronomy, meditating day and night, quiet and at ease, eating the good fruit of their deeds, fat and lush. Heaven forbid! This is not to be believed and does not come to mind except to the simple, who believe every word, who lean on their understanding. And properly, it is not incumbent on me to answer you. For what am I, to enter the innermost, into what I was not permitted to ponder, all the more so to answer questioners. But because it is a time to act for the LORD, I answer you from what I found written in the words of our Sages of blessed memory. May their merit stand for me, that no stumbling befall through me. Now, as for what you wrote, that you do not despise the sages of Israel, there are already several witnesses against you; you cannot deny it. And as for what brought you to this, that you attribute to them error and heresy: it is only because they are despised in your eyes. But a person should take heed for himself, lest he be burned by their coals, for the righteous are greater in their death than in their life, as they said in the Talmud. And as for what you wrote, that if one reveals the place of contradiction, and the Talmud also brings proof to refute the words of those greater than them, the case is not comparable to the proof, for where do we find that they bring proof to refute a halakhah given to Moses at Sinai? And the sages of Kabbalah say that thus they received from the mouth of Moses, and who is this one, and where is he, who gave you permission to inquire and investigate after their words? And as for what you wrote, that they call the partzufim divinities, God forbid, that they say thus. And as for what you wrote, go and learn from the intention of the blessings and the prayers. They already explained that the Cause of all causes is designated in a certain sefirah by such a name, and in a certain sefirah by that name. And as for what you wrote, that the Kabbalists explained that there are several worlds, thousands of thousands, etc., even if they were millions of millions, since they say that their Creator is one, and He gives life to all of them: what loss is there from this? And as for what you wrote, that they are in the image of a man possessing stature, already they said, "Great is the power of the prophets, who liken the likeness of the Power above to the form of a man." And as for what you wrote about 248 limbs, they already explained what the limbs are. For they are 216 letters of the Name of 72 and 32 paths, which allude to divine powers. And as for what you wrote, that I already conceded that my opinion is that there is no prayer applicable to the Cause of all causes, you speak falsehood. But surely, from the beginning of your question to me about the words of the Mesharef, I answered you, see in Kisse Eliyahu. But our Kabbalah holds that prayer is to Ein Sof and to bestow the flow upon the ten sefirot, as Lechem Shelomo wrote. And as for what I told you, to consult Kisse Eliyahu, so that you would know that the words of the Mesharef are words of heresy, in truth, and fitting to root it out. And God forbid that there be found in any book words like his, but the words of Kisse Eliyahu are not like his, God forbid. For the words of Kisse Eliyahu hold that Ze'ir Anpin is nothing but a vessel for the action of the Creator. And as for what he wrote on folio 25, that when we call upon Ze'ir Anpin, we call upon all the partzufim, with a soul hidden in them, which is Ein Sof, blessed be He. This does not mean that prayer is not directed to Ein Sof, Heaven forbid, but it means that the ascent of prayer to Ein Sof, blessed be He, is by way of this attribute. And the proof for this is what he wrote on folio 17b, and these are his words: "As for what is written about the intentions of prayer and the blessings, to direct in each blessing a particular intention, to a particular sefirah, not, God forbid, to the essence of the sefirah. For it is a cutting off, God forbid, and Heaven forbid to direct it to any particular power or particular sefirah. But all is to the essence of the one Ein Sof, blessed be He, the totality of all the powers, all of them." And furthermore he wrote on folio 25a: "And all our prayers are to Ein Sof, may He be blessed. Except that we cannot call Him by any appellation and name. Therefore we pray through the sefirot. For there is the applicability of all, all the appellations and names. For all the appellations and names are names of His essence, extending through the sefirot." Also he wrote on folio 26: "And if they do not do so, and do not dedicate their prayer solely to Ze'ir Anpin, they will not be answered." And all the Kabbalists lay down this principle, and these are their words: "As for whatever you find in some book of theirs, that prayer is addressed to any sefirah, Heaven forbid that it be so. But the intention is that one intend to raise them to Ein Sof by way of that sefirah."

Grammar
  • The paragraph is the respondent's reply in chapter 2. "You" is the questioner; the reply takes up each point of his letter in turn, introduced by ומה שכתבת ("as for what you wrote") and answered after it.
  • The rhetorical questions opened by וכי ("Can it be that ...", 2:28.56, 2:28.80, 2:28.96) and the sentences ending in a question mark (2:28.102, 2:28.106, 2:28.260, 2:28.279, 2:28.337) keep their question form; the text gives no answer to them within the paragraph.
  • Quotations of the Kabbalists are in double quotation marks. They open after the formula וז"ל (2:28.501, 2:28.601) or after כ' with a folio (2:28.539, 2:28.580), and close at the end of each passage, since the text gives no closing formula. The quoted words are Hebrew, except כיילי כללא דא (2:28.598-600), which is Aramaic and is rendered by its sense.
  • The verb ייחדו (2:28.589) is rendered "dedicate": to set the prayer apart for one addressee, the sense that fits אלא ("only"). "Unify" in the Kabbalistic sense is the alternative (see the review question); לז"א (2:28.592) is the entity the prayer is dedicated to.
  • Two Biblical allusions carry the opening and the close of the argument: Prov 16:1 at the start (2:28.1-7), and the word לה' from Ps 119:126 (2:28.172), which the author reads as "for the LORD".
  • אין הנדון דומה לראיה (2:28.249-252) is a fixed idiom of argument: the case under discussion is not like the case cited as proof, so the proof does not apply. לפני ולפנים (2:28.158-159) is the idiom for the innermost part (of the Temple), literally "before and within".

Prose paragraph: the respondent's reply in chapter 2. Each word is glossed. Letter numerals are given as Arabic numerals (רמ"ח 248, רי"ו 216, ע"ב 72, ל"ב 32, כ"ה 25, י"ז ע"ב 17b). Kisse Eliyahu and Lechem Shelomo are book titles; Ein Sof and Ze'ir Anpin are kept as names.

  • Isa 6:13 (allusion, 2:28.46-47): "זֶרַע קֹדֶשׁ", "the holy seed".
  • Isa 65:2 (allusion, 2:28.97-100): "בְּדֶרֶךְ לֹא־טוֹב", "in a way that is not good".
  • Ps 92:15 (allusion, 2:28.129-130): "דְּשֵׁנִים וְרַעֲנַנִּים", "fat and luxuriant".
  • Avot 2:10 (allusion, 2:28.224-225): the author's "פן יכוה בגחלתן" recalls the saying to beware of the coals of the sages; the words are his, not a quotation.

  • המשרף (2:28.402, 2:28.427): not a person here. In 3:10 and 3:12 the questioner is charged with calling the book Metzaref ha-Emunah ("Refiner of Faith") "the book Mesharef" and "Mesharef ha-Emunah" ("Burner of Faith"), from שרף "burn": a play on מצרף. The transliteration "Mesharef" is kept.

2:29

I have gone on at length about all this, to reconcile for you the words of Kisse Eliyahu, but my tradition I have already mentioned above. And there is proof from this that what you ask me is not from the motive of your request for the truth, as you said, but rather to seek some pretext. And who am I that you should hold me to be a Kabbalist, for I am brutish and do not know. And all my prayers are not even like the chirping of birds, for the birds are fed without distress, and on them there lies neither the yoke of kingship nor the yoke of worldly occupation, and chirping can be done with intent, but I, under so much burden of the times and the cares of livelihood, have my mind and my thoughts confused. And furthermore, I have not received from a wise Kabbalist mouth to mouth. Would that the LORD relieve me of the troubles of time and of livelihood, and provide me a Kabbalist master who would set me on the paths of uprightness, and that I might merit to be among the sons of ascent. As for what I answered you the second time, it is the words of Kisse Eliyahu that you turned a blind eye to. And as for what you wrote, that you do not ascribe corporeality to the sefirot, but did you not write: "If so, there would be a force in a body"? And this time you say that light is a subtle body. And I already wrote to you that what they called them by the name light is only in order to accommodate the ear; one time you ascribe corporeality and another time you make excuses. And why do all these doubts come into your mind, except because you ascribe corporeality? As for what you wrote: "Who is it that governs all these hidden worlds?" The one who brings them into being is the one who keeps them alive. And as for what you wrote, that Ze'ir Anpin is found to be the god of the lower ones. Have I not written to you that he is nothing but a tool for the acts of the Creator? And as for what you wrote, that some of them said "all the great work of the LORD," from which it follows that there is a small one? Those who say so have themselves already explained that they meant Metatron, whose name is like his master's, as they said in the Talmud: "And to Moses He said, 'Come up to the LORD'; it should have said 'to Me'. But this is Metatron, whose name is like his master's"; and so it is in the Yalkut. And as for what you wrote, that our true rabbis said, it is cited in Menorat ha-Ma'or that at the time of the giving of the Torah the Holy One, blessed be He, tore 7 heavens, etc. And in Midrash Rabbah they said: "I am the LORD your God; I am the first and I am the last. I am the first, for I have no father, and I am the last, for I have no son; and besides Me there is no God, for I have no brother." Who is it that says he has a father, or a son, or a brother? Rather, you spread slander against the sages who say so, and they have already explained their words, of blessed memory, that all the epithets and the attributes are in the sefirot, to accommodate the ear. Go now and see what Mahari Gikatilia wrote in the introduction to Sha'arei Orah, and the divine Rabbi Menachem Rikanti, and Rabbi Y. Chayyim, and these are his words: "In sum, wherever you see things that are not fitting to say of the Creator, may He be blessed, such as measure of stature and the like, it is all said of the sefirot; and when you see them speak in the manner of praise and thanksgiving, it is all said of the Creator, may He be blessed, who is within them and outside them, for nothing limits Him; therefore one may not say of the Creator, may He be blessed, not right and not left, not face and not back, etc." See there. And as for what you wrote, that the opinion of the Kabbalists is that the sefirot descend in a chain, by nature like a son from the father, far be it that they said so. On the contrary, they said: "Far be it to believe or to bring to mind that the sefirot are part of Ein Sof that came out of it and descended from cause to effect, for it is a criminal sin. For Ein Sof is not divided into parts, God forbid, and it receives no addition and no diminution, but its existence is constant always, without any change whatever, and He originated them, an absolute origination."

Grammar
  • The paragraph is the respondent's reply to his questioner, in the respondent's own voice. 'You' is the questioner, and the English keeps the second person.
  • Each point of the questioner's letter is answered in turn, opening with 'as for what you wrote' (2:29.101, 112, 160, 173, 187, 230, 373). The questions with 'but did you not' and 'and why' keep their force as questions.
  • Clauses with 'that' after 'you wrote' are reported speech and take no quotation marks. 'You wrote: if so ...' and 'you wrote: who is it ...' quote the questioner's own words, so they are in quotation marks.
  • The Talmud passage turns on the word 'to Me' (אלי): the verse should have said 'to Me', and the Talmud draws its conclusion from the difference. The English gives the Hebrew point in single quotation marks inside the double ones. 'אלי מבעי ליה' is Aramaic in the Talmud's wording; מכלל דאיכא קטן is Aramaic too.
  • The verb 'to ascribe corporeality' (להגשים) and its forms run through the paragraph. It is the error the writer charges against the questioner, and it is rendered the same way each time.
  • The idiom לשבר את האזן (2:29.143-145, 301-303), 'to break the ear', means to accommodate the ear, that is, to bring a matter within what the hearer can take in. The respondent uses it twice for the Kabbalists' physical epithets.

The respondent's reply (2:29) in the respondent's voice. Honorifics, book titles and abbreviations are rendered by the decisions for this work; see the notes at the first occurrence of each.

Other readings (3)
  • קבלתי: I received verb reading קבלתי as a verb: 'but I received, I already mentioned it above'; the English takes the noun 'my tradition'.
  • תפלותי: my foolish talk alternative spelling תפלות 'foolishness' has the same consonants; the English takes 'prayers' from the context.
  • בם: in them printed text The printed בם is 'in them'; the English reads the likelier בן, 'son'.
Apparatus

  • Bible verses: Exod 20:2 ('I am the LORD your God', 2:29.249-251, in the Midrash quotation); Isa 44:6 ('I am the first and I am the last, and besides Me there is no God', 2:29.252-271); Exod 24:1 ('And to Moses He said: Come up to the LORD', 2:29.213-218, in the Talmud quotation); Deut 11:7 ('all the great work of the LORD', 2:29.191-194); Ps 73:22 ('I am brutish and do not know', 2:29.38-40); Prov 4:11 ('the paths of uprightness', 2:29.95-96).
  • Variant: the printed 'בם' (2:29.279), 'in them'. Read as 'בן' (son), the likelier word in 'a father or a son or a brother'. The printed word is kept in the Hebrew; the English follows the sense.
  • The Talmud and Midrash passages carry no reference in the text, and none is added.
  • The quotation 'In sum ...' ends at 2:29.371 and is followed by 'See there' (2:29.372). The quotation 'Far be it ...' closes at 2:29.430.
  • Bible allusions: 'a criminal sin' (2:29.406-407) is Job 31:28 ('this too is a criminal sin'; cf. 31:11); 'spread slander' (2:29.284-285) is Num 14:36 ('and they spread slander') and Prov 10:18.
2:30

As for what you wrote, that Ze'ir Anpin is the son of Abba and Imma, and that he is the father of the effects that come after him, and he has a sister, his Nukva; all of it is a parable and an allusion concerning the sefirot. As for what you wrote, that no partzuf is to be worshipped, this is known on the lips of all the Kabbalists, and they have no need of your warning. As for what you wrote in the name of the Rambam: "Five are those called heretics, etc." Who is the one who says there is no God, or that there are two, or that He has a body, or that He is not the One alone, or that he worships another besides Him in order to be an intercessor, or the one who says he found ingredients, or the one who says the world was created something from something, God forbid. But a grudge has already risen in your heart, and you study the holy books, take the words in their plain sense, and rely on your understanding. And you forgot what the wisest of the wise said: "and do not lean on your understanding." Since you have already informed me that you understand, resolve my doubts, which I sent you and which I am about to send. As for what you wrote, that you understood that many and great men of wise heart, early and late, withdraw from it: God forbid that there be any sage who withdraws from it. And if there is one who withdraws from it, he himself admits openly that it is from his lack of knowledge of it. As for what you wrote, as the Ribash and the Chavot Yair wrote, you speak falsehood about them. And they are two valid witnesses to testify against you that you speak lies. And these are the words of the Ribash, in brief: "that Rabbi Peretz ha-Kohen did not speak of those sefirot and did not attach importance to them. Also he heard from his mouth that Rabbi Shimshon of Kinon used to say: 'I pray according to the understanding of this child,' that is, to remove from the hearts of the Kabbalists the idea that they pray at one time to one sefirah and at another time to another sefirah. Also in the Eighteen Benedictions they have, in each and every one, an intention toward a known sefirah. And all this is a very strange thing in the eyes of anyone who is not a Kabbalist like them, and they think it is the belief in duality. And he heard one of the would-be philosophers speaking in disparagement of the Kabbalists, and he would say: 'The Christians are believers in the Trinity, and the Kabbalists are believers in the tens.' And he asked the elderly sage Don Yosef ibn Shushan, who was a sage in the Talmud, who had looked into philosophy and was a Kabbalist, pious, great, and scrupulous in the commandments. And he said to him: 'How is it that you Kabbalists direct one blessing to one known sefirah and another blessing to another sefirah. Furthermore, is it so that there are divinities for the sefirot? That a man should pray to them?' And they answered him: 'God forbid that the prayer be anything but to the Name, may He be blessed, the Cause of causes; but one directs the thought to draw the flow to that sefirah which relates to the thing he asks for, just as you would say that in the blessing for the righteous one should direct to the sefirah called Chesed, which is the attribute of mercy, etc.' And he brought him a parable on this. He answered and said: 'And behold, very good.' And he said: 'I do not thrust myself into that wisdom, since I did not receive it from the mouth of a Kabbalist sage. And if I have seen commentaries on the secrets of the Ramban, they reveal a handbreadth and cover handbreadths.' And he said that a certain sage explained the Kabbalah not as the Ramban holds, and therefore he said that the words of that sage shall be his alone." And he ended his words. Therefore I say that one must not rely on such words, except from the mouth of a Kabbalist sage.

Grammar
  • This paragraph is the respondent's letter, answering the questioner in the second person. Each point opens with ומה שכתבת ('as for what you wrote') and is answered in turn.
  • The Ribash passage opens with the formula וז"ל and is given in double quotation marks; it closes at לבדו, and וחתם דבריו ('and he ended his words') is the respondent's closing formula outside the marks. The speakers inside it are in single quotation marks.
  • ואל בינתך אל תשען (Prov 3:5) is a verse quoted as a saying. תשען is the imperfect with אל, a negative command: 'do not lean'.
  • שאין לעבוד is impersonal: 'one may not worship', rendered 'that no partzuf is to be worshipped'.
  • היה with the participle (היה אומר) gives a habitual past: 'used to say'.
  • לדעת זה התינוק can be read as an infinitive ('to know this child') or as a construct ('according to the understanding of this child'); the English takes the construct (see `readings`).

The paragraph is in the respondent's voice. The quotation from the Ribash opens at וז"ל and closes at לו לבדו; וחתם דבריו is the respondent's closing formula and stands outside the marks. 'The Christians' renders הנצרים and 'something from something' renders יש מיש, both by the ruling. 'Ingredients' renders סמנים, the materials of the world's making. The Kabbalists' answer in the story is kept as Don Yosef's account gives it.

Other readings (2)
  • לדעת זה התינוק: to know this child plain infinitive לדעת as the infinitive 'to know', with זה התינוק as its object; the English reads the construct, 'according to the understanding of this child'.
  • המתפלספים: the philosophizers literal participle המתפלספים without the nuance of pretence that the hitpael form can carry.
Apparatus
  • Base text from Wikisource; the 1931 scan is not yet collated (Q2).
  • Prov 3:5: 'ואל בינתך אל תשען' ('and do not lean on your understanding'), quoted as the sage's words.
  • Gen 1:31: 'והנה טוב מאד' ('and behold, it was very good') is echoed in the answer 'והנה טוב מאד'.
  • Exod 28:3: 'חכמי לב' ('the wise of heart') is echoed in 'חכמי לב הפורשים ממנה'.
  • The text writes הנצרים (Notzrim) for the Christians; the decisions fix 'the Christians'.
2:31

Have you seen, to know that the Ribash's not getting involved in it is due to his not having received it from mouth to mouth, not due to any qualm as you say? And here you have the wording of the second witness, the Gaon, the author of Chavot Yair, of blessed memory, in very great brevity who was asked by a certain sage who spent his days in the Gemara and the decisors, and behold, a spirit rose within him and stirred him to study the Kabbalah for the exceeding excellence of its virtues, which is the soul of the Torah, and he saw several sayings of the Zohar that it is impossible to enter before the Holy King except by it, and the sages of the Talmud did not command about it, only warned not to expound it, "Do not inquire into what is too wondrous for you, etc." and he asked the Rabbi to free him from confusion, and he answered and said to him, "Woe is me if I advise you about withdrawal and cause slackening of hands and hindrance from this wisdom, which is without doubt the soul of the Torah and the root of faith, like wisdom and knowledge and understanding, and without doubt, whoever merits it is of the sons of ascent; happy is he, how good is his portion, and how pleasant is his greatness, beloved on high, etc." He cited the words of Yish'ar of Candia who went at very great length and gathered like sheaves to the threshing floor most of the opinions that preceded him to bring near and not to distance, against the book Bechinat ha-Dat, which sought to lead many astray! And he said that he found a peg fixed in a pillar of iron in a firm place to hang on to agree to receive a reward for withdrawal more than for inquiry in the book Shemen la-Ma'or, of the father of the Rav and these are his words, briefly: "And this matter that he wrote in the name of Rabbi Meir Gabbai, that everyone who has not received the secrets of the Torah from his master and thinks to weigh them in his mind transgresses the prohibition 'you shall not make for yourself a graven image', I said in my heart to call attention to the ways of people in our generation, I have seen infants who have not seen light, who say 'I am warm, I have seen light', hidden within them like leaven, chicks whose eyes had not opened, etc. And even the great ones on earth, whoever is sharp and diligent, expert in the chambers of the Torah, there is no strength in his intellect to grasp the chambers of light, except from the mouth of an elder and teacher. And these are the words of the Ramban in his introduction to the commentary on the Torah: 'And I hereby bring in a faithful covenant and it gives proper counsel to everyone who looks into this book, that he not suppose a supposition and not think thoughts about any matter of all the hints that I write in the secrets of the Torah, for I inform faithfully that my words will not be grasped by any reason or understanding except from the mouth of a wise Kabbalist into the ear of an understanding recipient. And the supposition about them is a folly of many harms, preventing benefit, etc.' And if you say that the commentary of the Ramban is different, since all his words are brief, by allusion, unlike other books of Kabbalah that explained their words, do you not see in Sha'arei Orah that he wrote on every page the phrase 'I hereby allude'? So too, in the book of Bachya, he was very brief and was accustomed to say in his own words 'and the wise will understand,' all the more so the book of the Zohar, which is closed and locked, and these are the words of Etz Chayyim in his introduction: 'Although certainly in the later generations they are sustained from this composition. There is no doubt that the waters of wisdom will not be revealed to any man by the power of contemplation according to their human intellect but only through a divine flow that flows upon him. And if the last of the Kabbalists went so far as to say that his words will not be grasped, how can it arise in the mind that human reason, especially of the people of our generation, this one, to understand and comprehend the words of the living God, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the voice of whose utterances is flames of fire and they are sealed with a thousand seals, etc. Therefore, men of understanding, hear me and do not break through to look at later books built according to their human intellect.' See there. And in my opinion, when a man sins in the musing of thought about the World of Emanation, his iniquity is too great to bear. Although many, and likewise perfect ones, of the later Kabbalists aroused the hearts of people greatly to the study of the Kabbalah and wrote that the one who withholds himself from studying Kabbalah is thrust out from his precinct and loses his world. It seems to me that they do not disagree, and surely whoever can learn from the mouth of a divine Kabbalist who will explain the matters to him as the Ari did for his disciples happy is his portion. And although the later ones permitted study from the books and understanding from one's own mind, 'better is the fingernail of the early ones, etc.' and 'sit and do not do' is better, for the danger to the body is graver, and all the more so to the soul, etc. And we may not inquire into hidden things but only to hear in the study of the plain meaning of Scripture and the reproof of moral instruction, to walk in the ways of the upright, for our knowledge is limited." Thus far the words of Shemen la-Ma'or, the proof from which is to agree to withdrawal, etc. And with all this I have revealed to you my opinion and do not rely on me, neither you nor another, for I am not fit to decide. And behold, I liken the study of this holy of holies to a journey to the Holy Land, for its virtue is known, as they said in the Talmud, that without it he is like one who has no God and like a worshipper of idols, and one who walks four cubits in the Land of Israel is a son of the world to come, and many praises. And even so, the Tosafot wrote in the name of Rabbi Chayyim that now it is not a commandment to dwell in the land, for there are many commandments dependent on the land which we are unable to fulfil, and further because of the danger of the roads, and because of the poverty there, which will lead him to transgress against his own will and the will of his Maker there. And if there is no expert before him and an excellent protection from all harm, it is good to refrain from this! Surely, too, who would deny the excellence of this wisdom, raised on high beyond compare, on condition that one who merits it learns it from the mouth of a Kabbalist who also received it from his master? And indeed it is true that I am astonished at books composed by later authors that brought sayings of the Zohar. And they raise difficulties about them and explain them according to their own judgment. Who gave permission to human reason to invent from the weighing of its own judgment the existence of three first ones and three tzachtzachot? For it is explained in the Zohar that there is a place that is not open to question, etc. and there is no proof from the saying of the Zohar and Sefer Yetzirah and R. M., who received from the mouth of the Elder of Elders and Elijah and the supernal holy ones, and all those children in the Zohar, the spirit of the LORD spoke through them and His word was on their tongue, and also the Ari and his disciples, who received from him mouth to mouth—from the mouth of the supernal ones the words came forth— and we, in our study of them, nothing comes to our mind except the reading of the words, which is not so with these later ones and with those who explain from their own judgment.

Grammar
  • The paragraph is one long period built on ו. The author's own voice carries the whole: the Gaon's reply (double marks), Shemen la-Ma'or (double marks, opened by וז"ל and closed by ע"כ at token 523), and inside Shemen the Ramban and Etz Chayyim (single marks) and shorter sayings (single marks). The closing formulas stand outside the marks.
  • הראית is ה (the question particle) with ראית 'you saw': 'Have you seen ... ?'. The clause מה שלא נתקע הריב"ש בה is the subject of הוא מחמת: 'the Ribash's not getting involved in it is due to ...'. שאתה האומר is 'as you, the sayer'.
  • Aramaic in the paragraph: Zohar Aramaic in דאי אפשר ליעול קמי מלכא קדישא ('that it is impossible to enter before the Holy King') and דאית מקום דלא קימא לשאלה; Talmudic Aramaic in דזכי לה ('whoever merits it'), שאני ('is different'), לא פליגי ('they do not disagree'), ואע"ג ('and although') and דחמירא סכנתא דגופא ('for the danger of the body is graver').
  • Three sentences have their main clause after a Hebrew full stop (ואם תאמר ... הלא תראה; ואע"ג ... טוב ציפורנם; ואפי' הגדולים ... אין כח בשכלו). They are joined with a comma, as the rulings provide, and a token note says so. Two later sentences (ועוד, בתנאי, כי יש, וגם האר"י) continue a list and are joined in the same way.
  • שאני פי' הרמב"ן: שאני is Aramaic 'is different' and פי' is פירוש 'commentary', so 'the commentary of the Ramban is different'. The speaker's objection is that the Ramban was brief by allusion, unlike books that explain; the reply is the question הלא תראה בשערי אורה.
  • Several phrases echo verses and are translated in the verse's sense: סגור ומסוגר, אשר בארץ, כעמיר גורנה, יתד תקוע במקום נאמן, אנשי לבב שמעו לי, ואל תהרסון לראות, גדול עונו מנשוא, רוח ה' דבר בם ומלתו על לשונם (see apparatus).
Other readings (3)
  • נתקע הריב"ש בה: the Ribash was not fixed in it plain nif'al of תקע, be fixed the literal sense behind 'did not get involved in it'
  • לכל אדם: to every man plain לא before לכל 'not to every man' (some might) against 'not to any man'; the following אלא (only through the flow) favours 'any'
  • נעים גודלו: how pleasant is his lot printed word גודלו read as גורלו see apparatus
Ancient Near East
  • The Ribash is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Sheshet.
  • The Ari is Rabbi Yitzchak Luria (Isaac Luria), the sixteenth-century Kabbalist of Safed.
  • Candia is the Venetian name of Heraklion on Crete; Yish'ar of Candia is named after it.
Apparatus
  • Base text: Wikisource (the 1931 scan has not been collated; Q2 default: Wikisource additions are translated as base text, flagged here until collated).
  • פה אל פה (2:31.12-14, 721-725): Num 12:8, the idiom of direct oral tradition.
  • Isa 44:16 אח חמותי ראיתי אור (2:31.212-215): 'I am warm, I have seen the fire'; the author's text has אור and the sense 'light' follows לא ראו אור (Job 3:16, עללים לא ראו אור, 'infants who never saw light').
  • Printed word: נתפתהו (2:31.221); the likelier word is נתפקחו or נפתחו, 'were opened'. Translated by the sense of the context.
  • 2 Sam 7:9 (1 Chr 17:8) כשם הגדולים אשר בארץ (2:31.225-227): echo; 'the great ones on earth'.
  • Mic 4:12 כי קבצם כעמיר גרנה (2:31.134-136): 'He has gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor'.
  • Isa 22:23, 25 יתד תקוע במקום נאמן (2:31.152-159): 'a peg driven in a firm place'; Jer 1:18 עמוד ברזל (2:31.154-155): 'a pillar of iron'.
  • Exod 20:4 (Deut 5:8) לא תעשה לך פסל (2:31.194-197): 'You shall not make for yourself a graven image'.
  • Printed word: גודלו (2:31.124); the likelier word is גורלו 'his lot' (liturgy: מה טוב חלקנו ומה נעים גורלנו). Translated as printed, 'his greatness'.
  • Dan 12:10 והמשכילים יבינו (2:31.337-338): echo in Bachya's formula והמשכיל יבין.
  • Josh 6:1 סגרת ומסגרת (2:31.343-344): possible echo of סגור ומסוגר, 'closed and locked'.
  • Jer 23:36 דברי אלהים חיים (2:31.396-398): 'the words of the living God'.
  • Ps 29:7 קול ה' חצב להבות אש (2:31.401-404): echo; 'the voice ... flames of fire'.
  • Job 34:10 לכן אנשי לבב שמעו לי (2:31.410-414): 'Therefore, men of understanding, hear me'.
  • Exod 19:21 (also 19:24) פן יהרסו אל ה' לראות (2:31.415-417): 'lest they break through ... to look'; the sense of הרס there is 'break through'.
  • Gen 4:13 גדול עוני מנשוא (2:31.434-436): 'my iniquity is too great to bear'.
  • Deut 29:28 הנסתרות (2:31.508): echo; Prov 6:23 תוכחות מוסר (2:31.515-516): 'reproofs of discipline'.
  • 2 Sam 23:2 רוח ה' דבר בי ומלתו על לשוני (2:31.711-717): 'The spirit of the LORD spoke through me, His word was on my tongue', with the plural 'them'.
  • Isa 58:11 בצחצחות: the only biblical occurrence of the word, in another sense ('parched places'); the Kabbalists' term (2:31.683) is not that sense.
  • Quotations of the Talmud, the Zohar and Ben Sira in the paragraph carry no reference in the Hebrew, and none is added.
2:32

And behold, my beloved, like my brother of blessed memory, the parable of the land of Israel, the referent, for the long journey toward the place of the Name in the grasp of the secret is the shortness of the one who grasps and the depth of what is grasped, and the multitude of propositions, which are preventing causes in every grasp of wisdom, and especially in the wisdom of Kabbalah, in several respects, and over all of them is the sin, which obstructs and separates between the intellect and the intelligible, etc., and indeed, even though the author of Pardes Rimonim, because of the greatness of his holiness and his piety, is very careful in many places, and warns greatly against a strange thought that is of division, and limit, and the composing of parables, etc., we too shall say: would that a spirit from on high be poured out upon us, that we might grasp and understand the matters without inclining from the truth and from the roots of the religion, etc. And by these, take this rule in your hand: all things that are forbidden in the books of the Kabbalists, which they mentioned without dispute on the matter and without inquiry, and their plain sense will be understood, and the joining of the things: bind them on a white tablet, and let them be frontlets between your eyes. And even when things are read before you that appear astonishing in themselves, or from the side that it seems, God forbid, that there is division, number, corporeality and change, you shall accept them in the faith of an artisan, and say in your heart that your mind is short, and your knowledge in the depth of understanding, without your doubting, God forbid, one of the roots of the religion that are stated in Yigdal and in several places, for even those fundamental ones, it is not possible to descend to their roots by human reason, etc. And now go and learn that it is forbidden to innovate and to understand a matter from what is written in the book, lest he not aim at the truth, however, to explain verses according to what the Kabbalists said, that the premise is agreed; only that on this he explains the verse, or says that there is an allusion in it, by means of gematria, or the initial and final letters of words. It is good and fine that he only say it as a possibility, without deciding the matter, etc., only let him not waste his time on them, and whatever the LORD has put in his heart, and it is well reasoned, sound, without strain, he should not cast it behind his back, but rather let him write it down for memory, and let it be in his eyes as one who finds great spoil, for it is a sign for his soul, a portion of God from on high, which has nourishment and access in a high place, and he will be called holy, and now, behold, I have revealed to you the secrets of my heart. And you, the king, in your reflection and your knowledge, holy and broad, tell me, please, your ways, and I will set aside my opinion before your opinion. Yair Chayyim Bakhrakh.

Grammar
  • One long period runs from the opening to 'etc.' (2:32.44). Its subject is 'the long journey toward the place of the Name in the grasp of the secret'; its predicate is 'is the shortness of the one who grasps and the depth of what is grasped'. The list that follows (the propositions, the sin) hangs on the same clause.
  • 'Even when' (2:32.117-118, ואף כי) and 'even though' (2:32.46-47, והנה אף כי) open concessive clauses. The main clause of the first is at 2:32.135-139, and of the second at 2:32.68-70 'we too shall say'. The English keeps the Hebrew's order, and has no full stop where the Hebrew has none (2:32.44, 2:32.67).
  • 'Would that' is the optative 'who will give' (2:32.71-72). 'And be poured out' (2:32.73) is the wish, and 'that we might grasp' (2:32.77) is its purpose clause, with the verb in the form שנשכיל.
  • Imperatives and jussives: 'take' (2:32.88), 'go and learn' (2:32.169-170), 'let them be' (2:32.113), 'let him write it' (2:32.239). 'He should not cast' (2:32.234-235) is a negative command with אל.
  • Passive forms, each rendered passive: 'will be understood' (2:32.103), 'are read' (2:32.119), 'is well reasoned' (2:32.230; a passive participle), 'what is written' (2:32.176), 'is agreed' (2:32.192).
  • 2:32.259-261 echoes Isa 4:3 (קדוש יאמר לו): יאמר is passive, 'he shall be called holy'. ממשל / הנמשל (2:32.5, 2:32.8) are the pair mashal and nimshal: a parable and what it stands for.

Single prose paragraph in the writer's own voice, addressed to a correspondent ('my beloved'; 'you, the king'). The English follows the Hebrew's order. Where the Hebrew has no full stop (2:32.44, 2:32.67), the English has none. Choices bearing on the words are in apparatus or readings: ממשל / הנמשל (2:32.5-8, the parable and its referent), גיוו (2:32.237, 'back' or 'inner part'), and the signature surname (2:32.284), whose vowels are a guess. Open for the editor: the signature is that of Yair Chayyim Bakhrakh, whom 2:31 introduces ('the Gaon, author of Chavot Yair') and 2:33 cites ('he himself said: would that a spirit ... be poured out upon us'), so 2:32 may be the close of his quoted letter, not the author's own words; the English has no quotation marks.

Other readings (1)
  • ממשל ארץ ישראל הנמשל: the ruler of the land of Israel, the one ruled alternative reading of the word ממשל as the noun 'rule, ruler' and הנמשל as 'the one ruled'; not adopted, because the next sentence explains a referent, and 2:31 is about walking in the Land of Israel.
Ancient Near East
  • Pardes Rimonim (Pomegranate Orchard) is a Kabbalistic book. The paragraph refers to its author without naming him.
Apparatus
  • Base text: Wikisource. The 1931 scan is not yet collated, and Wikisource additions are translated as base text and flagged here (Q2).
  • 'ויערה עלינו רוח ממרום' (2:32.73-76): allusion to Isa 32:15, 'until a spirit be poured out upon us from on high'.
  • 'לטטפות בין עיניך' (2:32.114-116): allusion to Deut 6:8, 'and they shall be frontlets between your eyes'.
  • 'קשרם על לוח לבן' (2:32.109-112): allusion to Prov 3:3, which reads 'the tablet of your heart' (לוח לבך). The author writes לבן, 'white', and the English follows his wording.
  • 'כמוצא שלל רב' (2:32.243-245): allusion to Ps 119:162, 'as one who finds great spoil'.
  • 'חלק אלוה ממעל' (2:32.250-252): allusion to Job 31:2, 'a portion of God from on high'.
  • 'גיוו' (2:32.237): 'back' or 'inner part'. The English takes the idiom 'behind his back', to ignore; the literal sense is in the token note.
  • 'הפ'' (2:32.197): read as 'the verse' by the rule for ס' before a verse. The author does not name the verse.
  • Signature (2:32.282-284): the surname בכרך is unvocalized. 'Bakhrakh' is a guess at the vowels, not a fixed form. The first two names are as written.
  • 'ממשל ארץ ישראל הנמשל' (2:32.5-8): read as 'the parable of the land of Israel, the referent' (mashal and nimshal). The alternative, 'the ruler of the land of Israel, the one ruled', is in readings and is not adopted.
  • 'וקדוש יאמר לו' (2:32.259-261): allusion to Isa 4:3, 'shall be called holy'.
  • 'הודיעני נא את דרכיך' (2:32.274-277): allusion to Exod 33:13, 'let me know Your ways', and Ps 25:4 'Your ways, LORD, make known to me'.
  • 'אל ישליך אחרי גיוו' (2:32.234-237): echoes 1 Kgs 14:9 (השלכת אחריך גוך) and Neh 9:26 (אחרי גום), 'behind his back'.
2:33

Have you seen, to know the words of the Gaon Chavot Yair, how afraid and trembling he is to teach about separation, and relies on the words of the Gaon, the author of Shemen la-Ma'or, whose words were cited above, yet he is still afraid to say it outright, lest it slacken the hands from engaging in this holy wisdom, and how much he praises this wisdom, for one who merits it, to learn it from the mouth of a Kabbalist, and admits that anyone who holds himself back from studying it, after receiving it, is pushed away from his precinct; and also he permits engaging in the words of Kabbalah, and if he sees puzzling things before him, he should accept them in the faith of an artisan, and attribute it to the shortness of his understanding. If so, your two witnesses, the Ribash and Chavot Yair, will testify and bear witness against you that you invent things from your own heart; and where is his separation, that he separated, as you said? Did he not himself say, "Would that a spirit from on high were poured upon us," etc.? And I bring you proof that he merited the wisdom of Kabbalah, for in section 172 he wrote, and these are his words: "that it is possible there are further matters of secret and concealment in two verses, 'two thousand bath it held' and 'three thousand baths,' for at the sin of the first man three alefs were corrupted, of truth, of Adonai and of man, and there remained mat-din-dam against idolatry, illicit unions and bloodshed. And King David repaired truth; therefore he did not taste sleep at night, and did not manage to repair judgment, and also blood, as the Holy One, blessed be He, said: 'You shall not build the house, for you have shed much blood; only your son Solomon, for peace, etc.' And Solomon repaired two alefs, and with the alef of his father, three alefs were repaired, and the matter of bat is known to the initiates, for the main flaw is there, and he further expanded on the secret of the matter there. And section 176, on the matter of one who feeds a man blind in one of his eyes, and with all this I protested, for it seems to me that in both cases there is room to distinguish. However, where there is another fitting and suitable one like him, for it is known that the 248 limbs are a throne and a likeness of the 248 supernal lights, and the 248 limbs of the soul. And so, in every such case the throne is flawed, for according to the hidden there are heaps upon heaps of secret mysteries in the parts of the body, and there is a lack of flow in the cup of blessing." The above-mentioned, too, in the colophon of the book, wrote that he made 635 responsa and gathered from them 232, the number of "Let there be light," and it has the gematria of the four fillings of YHVH, 72, 63, 45, 52: the son who is in Abba and Imma, and Ze'ir and his Nukva. And further, "Let there be light" is Yah ya'ir ("Yah will give light"). These are the sources of Tif'eret (Beauty) and Malkhut (Kingship) in Binah (Understanding), which is the light emanated on the first day. And he further expanded on many matters of secret and concealment. Also his father, the author of Shemen la-Ma'or, was a divine Kabbalist, for his verses were printed at the end of the book. And these are according to the Name of forty-two, and the twelve combinations of YHVH, and the twenty-four combinations of Adonai, and the Name of twenty-two. Also the true sage, the author of Menorat ha-Ma'or, was a divine Kabbalist, for in chapter 93 he wrote on "Baruch She'amar": "its way in it, the number of the ten, the ten, etc." And in chapter 95 he wrote: "Kaddish is not said with fewer than ten, and the reason is that with ten the holiness is completed, which is above the ten sefirot." And in chapter 133 he wrote: "When Jacob was going down to Egypt, he saw that the exile had begun in him and in his seed, and he feared it and sacrificed sacrifices to the Fear of his father Isaac, so that the attribute of judgment would not be stretched out against him; and did this at Beersheba, which is a house of prayer for his fathers, and offered peace-offerings to complete to him all the attributes, as they expounded: 'shelamim, which cast peace', to complete to him the attribute of Gevurah (Might)." And in chapter 147 he wrote: "It is found that the completeness of holiness is in the ten, which allude to the ten havayot, and they are the ten sayings by which the world was created." And in chapter 153 he wrote: "And in the way of truth, that in six days the LORD made, etc. and on the seventh day it is Sabbath, and it has no male mate, and the Assembly of Israel is its female mate, as it is said: 'and the earth,' and behold, it is the Eighth Day of Assembly, for there everything is held back. And this is their saying: 'The eighth is a festival in itself,' and it is the completion of the first, for it is the emanation of the first ones, and it is not in their unity, and whoever understands the havayot will be wise and find the truth." And in the colophon of the book he wrote: "And the fifth, I left out the grave matters, which are hidden and lofty, and there is no one who can attain them but a single individual in a generation." Thus he wished to write secret matters in his work, but because they are not fit for every person. Have you seen, to know that no one disputes the Kabbalah: neither the early ones nor the later ones, neither the many nor the individuals, neither the great nor the small. On the contrary, all agree that whoever merits Kabbalah from mouth to ear, there is no finer virtue for you than it, and that it is forbidden to expound and investigate it; but if he wishes, he should accept it in complete faith and not explain it by his human intellect. For he should attribute what troubles him to the shortness of his understanding, and not break through to think anything of the soul. And with this, all the words of the lowest of the low are complete. Seder. And you shall return and listen to the voice of the LORD.

Grammar
  • The opening and the closing both begin 'Have you seen, to know' (הראית לדעת, 1 and 538): the speaker addresses the questioner with a rhetorical question.
  • The quotation from Chavot Yair is opened by כתב וז"ל (115-116) and runs to 267; it includes the passage on section 176, whose 'I protested' (213) is the Gaon's own voice. The Holy One's words inside it (164-179) take single marks. The next sentence (268 on) is the author's own report.
  • לדזכי לה ללמדה (41-43): דזכי is Aramaic, 'who merits': 'for one who merits it, to learn it from the mouth of a Kabbalist'. פרישתו שפירש (90-91): the verb is pirash 'separated', of the same root as הפרישה (13).
  • The exegesis at 123-148 turns on alef: אלפין is the Aramaic plural of אלף, the letter. The three alefs are the first letters of אמת, אדנות and אדם; without them what remains is מת, דין and דם, 'mat-din-dam', set against idolatry, illicit unions and bloodshed. The two verses (1 Kgs 7:26, 2 Chr 4:5) speak of 'two thousand' and 'three thousand' baths; the author hears אלפים as 'two alefs'. בת is both the measure 'bath' and 'bat', 'daughter'.
  • שמיני רגל (488) is the Talmudic formula for the Eighth Day, which is Shemini Atzeret (481); the author argues from its separateness to the emanation of the first ones.
  • ולא יהרוס לחשוב (592-593): 'break through to think', as in Exod 19:21, 24; the sentence after a full stop that begins with שהם (300) is given a main clause ('These are'), as the ruling provides.

The paragraph is the respondent's rebuke of the questioner, in the respondent's voice. The quotation from Chavot Yair opens at 117 and closes at 267 (the end is inferred, since 268 resumes the author's report). Words the translator left open: העליון (268) is 'the above-mentioned'; לי"ח (193) is read, conjecturally, as ליודעי חן; לחשוב (593) is 'to think' after 'break through'; סדר (602) is left as 'Seder'. 'קראתי תיגר' (213) is the quoted Gaon's own protest.

Other readings (6)
  • לדזכי לה ללמדה מפי מקובל: that one may merit it by learning it from a Kabbalist plain
  • לענין הזן סומא באחת מעיניו: on the matter of the cantor who is blind in one of his eyes plain
  • מספר יהי אור: the book Yehi Or plain
  • בן שבאבא ואימא וזעיר ונוקביה: 52 (BaN), which are in Abba and Imma, and Ze'ir and his Nukva plain
  • ואת הארץ והנה: 'and the earth, and behold,' plain
  • ולא יהרוס לחשוב שום הנשמה: and not ruin any soul by thinking plain
Ancient Near East
  • Rabbi Isaac ben Sheshet (the Ribash) was a responsa author of the fourteenth century. Here he and Chavot Yair are 'your two witnesses', the authorities the questioner has cited for abstaining from Kabbalah.
  • Chavot Yair is the collection of responsa of Rabbi Yair Chayyim Bacharach (1638-1702); the author cites it by section number.
Apparatus
  • Base text from Wikisource; the 1931 scan is not yet collated, so the base text is translated as it stands.
  • Quotation boundaries: the Chavot Yair quotation, opened by כתב וז"ל (115-116), is taken to run from שאפשר (117) to the cup of blessing (267), including the passage on section 176; the Hebrew marks no closing formula, and the end is inferred because 268 (העליון ג"כ ... כ') resumes the author's own report. The quotations from Menorat ha-Ma'or have no formula either; each is closed where its passage ends.
  • Neh 6:8: מלבך אתה בודאם, echoed in בודה דברים מלבך (85-87).
  • Isa 32:15: עד יערה עלינו רוח ממרום, echoed in the Gaon's מי יתן ויערה עלינו רוח ממרום (98-103), in the author's wording.
  • 1 Kgs 7:26: אלפים בת יכיל (125-127); 2 Chr 4:5 for 'three thousand baths' (128-130), in the author's wording, which differs from the verse.
  • 1 Chr 22:8-9: the words 'לא תבנה הבית כי דמים רבים שפכת, רק בנך שלמה כי שלום' follow the author's wording, which differs from the verse.
  • Gen 1:3: יהי אור (280-281, 296-297), the phrase whose number is 232.
  • Gen 31:42: פחד יצחק, 'Fear of Isaac' as a divine epithet (400-402); Gen 46:1: ויזבח זבחים (398-399).
  • Exod 20:11: ששת ימים עשה ה' (457-460), cut short with וכו' (461); ואת הארץ (476-477) is the end of the same verse.
  • Exod 19:21, 24: פן יהרסו / ואל יהרסו, a possible echo in ולא יהרוס לחשוב (592-593).
  • Deut 30:8: ואתה תשוב ושמעת בקול ה' (603-607), exactly as the verse reads.
2:34

Reply. I ask of my God that He lead me in paths of straightness and rescue us from a lying lip, from a deceitful tongue. Teach me, LORD, Your ways; I will walk in Your truth. Unite my heart to fear Your name. And send Your light and Your truth; they will lead me to answer a word spoken in its settings. Roll reproach and scorn away from me, for I have kept Your testimonies. Even though princes sit and speak against me, Your servant meditates on Your statutes. Then I shall not be ashamed, when I do not turn aside from the way that our Rabbis of blessed memory taught us, the masters of the Mishnah and the Talmud and the true midrashim and the decisors who follow in their footsteps, on whom all the house of Israel lean. For they are the masters of the true tradition, who received from Moses our teacher the generalities and particulars of the Torah, upon which he stood at Sinai forty days and forty nights, and handed them to Joshua, and Joshua to the elders, etc., as is stated in tractate Avot. 1) And it is a holy duty incumbent on us to follow in their footsteps in everything that yields a practical difference in law: in all matters of forbidden and permitted, impure and pure, unfit and fit. All the more so in matters of the unity of the Name, may He be blessed, which is the great principle, and after it the tradition of all the commandments and how they are to be done, as the Tanna, peace be upon him, said: "Why did the section of Shema precede 'And it shall be, if you hearken, etc.!'" And any author of a book who comes to add to or subtract from their words, and all the more so to turn us from the faith of the holy Torah according to the tradition of our rabbis, the masters of the Mishnah and the Talmud, we will not hearken to him. And even if he performs signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, we will not turn aside from following the LORD our God, according to the tradition of our Rabbis of blessed memory, the masters of the Mishnah and the Talmud and the decisors who come after them and follow in their footsteps. And even if from heaven a bat kol calls, hearken to him, to depart from their tradition, we shall not heed it, as Rabbi Yehoshua said: "One does not heed a bat kol, for it is not in heaven."

Grammar
  • תשובה: the label of the reply, as at 2:3, 2:7 and 2:28 of the correspondence; אשאלה מאלהי ינחני: 'I will ask of my God that He lead me'; the paragraph is a prayer in the author's own voice, addressed to the LORD.
  • The Psalm verses are run into the author's sentences without a formula: הוריני (Ps 86:11), ושלח (Ps 43:3), גל (Ps 119:22) and גם כי ישבו (Ps 119:23), so they take no quotation marks.
  • אז לא אבוש כאשר לא אסור מן הדרך: the main clause is 'then I shall not be ashamed'; כאשר is a temporal clause, 'when I do not turn aside'.
  • אשר למדונו רז"ל ... בעלי המשנה ... ההולכים בעקבותיהם is a relative clause on הדרך: the way that the Sages taught us, with the authorities in apposition; אשר כל בית ישראל נשענים עליהם is a second relative clause on the same authorities.
  • The Tanna's question, 'למה קדמה פרשת שמע לוהיה אם שמוע וכו'!', is quoted in the author's words and truncated with וכו'; the author then argues a fortiori (וכ"ש) from matters of law to the unity of the Name, and from the unity to the rejection of an author who alters the tradition.
  • Aramaic idioms in the author's Hebrew: מידי דנפקא מינה לדינא ('what yields a practical difference in law') and לא משגחינן בה ('we do not heed it'); the Tanna's question about the Shema is Mishnaic Hebrew, and R. Yehoshua's saying is the Talmud's.

The author's prayer opens the paragraph, then his claim for the tradition of the Mishnah, Talmud and decisors. The English keeps 'us' where the Hebrew has ויצילנו; the Psalm allusions are in apparatus.

Ancient Near East
  • Bat kol (literally 'daughter of a voice') is the rabbinic term for a voice from heaven. The saying the author cites, by Rabbi Yehoshua, holds that such a voice is not heeded in matters of law, since it is not in heaven.
Apparatus
  • Base text from Wikisource; the 1931 scan is not yet collated (Wikisource additions, Q2).
  • Ps 120:2 (embedded): משפת שקר, מלשון רמיה. The psalm has 'my soul' where the author writes ויצילנו (us).
  • Ps 23:3 (embedded allusion): ינחני במעגלי צדק; the author writes יושר.
  • Ps 86:11 (embedded): הוריני ה' דרכיך אהלך באמתך; יחד לבבי ליראה שמך.
  • Ps 43:3 (embedded): ושלח אורך ואמתך המה ינחוני.
  • Prov 25:11 (embedded): דבר דבור על אופניו. The author prints אפניו; the verse has אופניו.
  • Ps 119:22: גל מעלי חרפה ובוז כי עדותיך נצרתי.
  • Ps 119:23: גם כי ישבו שרים בי נדברו, עבדך ישיח בחוקיך.
  • Ps 119:6 (embedded): אז לא אבוש.
  • Deut 11:13: והיה אם שמוע תשמעו, the opening of the second paragraph of the Shema; the author writes לוהיה.
  • Deut 13:2-5 (embedded allusion): אות ומופת; לא תשמע אל דברי הנביא ההוא; אחרי ה' אלהיכם תלכו.
  • Deut 10:10 (embedded allusion; cf. Deut 9:9): עמדתי בהר ... ארבעים יום וארבעים לילה.
  • Deut 30:12: לא בשמים היא, the verse on which Rabbi Yehoshua's saying rests.
  • 2:34.199 לבור (printed): probably לעבור, 'to pass from', with the ע dropped (cf. 'to depart from their tradition'); translated by the sense of the context. The Hebrew לבור does not mean 'depart'.
